faqs.question: How much does a website cost for a small business in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Most professionally built small business websites in Bangladesh cost between ৳18,000 and ৳1,50,000 in 2026. A basic 5–8 page brochure site runs ৳18,000–৳60,000, and a lead-generation site runs ৳65,000–৳1,50,000. E-commerce and custom platforms start around ৳1,50,000 and can exceed ৳5,00,000.

faqs.question: How much does it cost to build a business website in Bangladesh in US dollars?
faqs.answer: At roughly ৳123 per dollar, a basic Bangladeshi business website costs about 145–490, a lead-generation site about 530–1,220, and an e-commerce or custom platform about 1,220–4,065 or more. These figures are for professional builds by Dhaka agencies and freelancers, not for DIY subscriptions.

faqs.question: Why do website quotes vary so much between Bangladeshi agencies?
faqs.answer: Quotes vary because scope, design approach, platform, and team experience differ. A solo freelancer and a multi-person agency can both sell a website, but they deliver different design depth, testing, and support, which is why two proposals for what sounds like the same project can land far apart in price.

faqs.question: How much should I budget for website running costs each year?
faqs.answer: Budget roughly 10–20% of the build price per year on larger projects. In practice, yearly costs run ৳1,000–৳2,500 for a domain, ৳4,000–৳ 30,000+ for hosting, and ৳15,000–৳ 50,000+ for maintenance. SSL is often free with hosting or ৳3,000–৳15,000 for a premium certificate.

faqs.question: Is a ৳10,000 website good enough for a business?
faqs.answer: A ৳10,000 website can work as a simple online presence, but it usually means a template site from an entry-level freelancer with limited support. Experienced freelancers with a portfolio and basic post-launch support typically price closer to ৳15,000–৳25,000, which is usually a better investment for a business that depends on the site.

faqs.question: Can I build a business website myself to save money?
faqs.answer: Yes. DIY builders such as Wix, Squarespace, and WordPress.com cost about ৳1,200–৳12,000 a month and can work well for a simple brochure site. The trade-off is your own time and a lower ceiling on customization, SEO control, and scalability compared with a custom build.

faqs.question: How much does an e-commerce website cost in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: An agency-built e-commerce website in Bangladesh typically costs ৳1,50,000–৳5,00,000 or more. The price covers product catalogs, checkout, bKash and Nagad integration, and inventory management. Cheaper store setups exist, but they usually come with less support and fewer custom features.

Most professionally built small business websites in Bangladesh cost between ৳18,000 and ৳1,50,000 in 2026, roughly $145 to $1,220, depending on who builds the site and what it needs to do. That's the direct answer to how much a business website cost, and the sections below explain why the range is so wide.

Quotes for the same site can differ several times over, since the number on a proposal depends on who builds it, what it has to do, and what it costs to run after launch, not on any fixed market rate. 

Quick Answer: How Much Does a Business Website Cost in Bangladesh?

A professionally built business website in Bangladesh typically costs ৳18,000–৳60,000 for a basic 5–8 page brochure site, ৳65,000–৳1,50,000 for a lead-generation site, and ৳1,50,000–৳5,00,000 or more for e-commerce or custom platforms. Running costs add roughly 10–20% of the build price each year.

A business website is a multi-page site, typically Home, About, Services, and Contact pages, and often a blog, built to represent a company and generate leads or sales. It differs from a single landing page built around one offer and from a personal portfolio with no commercial goal.


What Kind of Website Do You Actually Need? (Quick Self-Diagnostic)

Business websites fall into three types: brochure sites of 3–8 pages that build credibility, lead-generation sites that add a blog and conversion tools, and e-commerce stores with product catalogs and checkout. The type sets the price floor more than any other single choice.

  1. Brochure site: Home, About, Services, and Contact pages that establish credibility and answer basic questions. Lead capture stops at a contact form.

  2. Lead-generation site: A brochure site plus a blog, service pages built around specific search terms, and conversion tools such as forms, calculators, or booking widgets.

  3. E-commerce site: A storefront with product catalogs, checkout, payment processing, and inventory management. In Bangladesh, that usually includes local payment options such as bKash and Nagad alongside cards.

A brochure site and an e-commerce store both quoted at ৳1,00,000 are not the same product, even though the number looks identical on a proposal.


Cost by Build Method: DIY, Freelancer, or Agency

In Bangladesh, a DIY builder costs about ৳1,200–৳12,000 a month, a solo freelancer typically ৳8,000–৳25,000 per site, a mid-tier Dhaka agency ৳18,000–৳1,50,000, and an established professional firm ৳1,50,000–৳5,00,000 or more for larger builds.

The cheapest end of the market carries a trade-off. Entry-level freelancers commonly price around ৳5,000–৳8,000, while experienced freelancers with an established portfolio typically price ৳15,000–৳25,000, and post-launch support and code quality typically differ meaningfully between the two tiers.


What Actually Drives the Price Up or Down

Four factors move a website quote the most: page count, design (template or custom), functionality such as e-commerce or booking, and integrations with payment, CRM, or marketing tools. Design and functionality changes are what push a project from freelancer pricing into agency pricing.

A template-based site changes colors and images on a ready-made layout, which is faster and cheaper. A custom design adds research, wireframes, and design hours, which raises the price. Blog systems, multilingual support in Bangla and English, and payment gateway integration such as bKash and Nagad typically have a medium impact on price, while e-commerce carts and custom modules have a high one.

The platform matters too. WordPress is often cheaper because many developers know it, while custom frameworks cost more because of specialized coding time. See WordPress, Webflow, or custom development for how that choice affects cost and flexibility.

One mistake people often make is comparing two quotes on price alone without checking that both include the same four factors. A ৳45,000 quote and a ৳45,000 quote can describe completely different scopes.


Hidden Costs Most Quotes Leave Out

Beyond the build fee, a Bangladeshi business website has yearly costs: domain ৳1,000–৳2,500, hosting ৳4,000–৳30,000 or more, SSL free or ৳3,000–৳15,000, and maintenance ৳15,000–৳50,000 or more. Quotes that list only the build fee leave these out.

  • Domain: ৳1,000–৳2,500 per year, renewed annually.

  • Hosting: ৳4,000–৳30,000 or more per year. Shared hosting suits basic sites, while cloud or dedicated hosting suits e-commerce and higher traffic.

  • SSL certificate: Often bundled free with hosting, or ৳3,000–৳15,000 per year for a premium certificate.

  • Maintenance and support: ৳15,000–৳50,000 or more per year for updates, backups, security fixes, and broken-link repairs. See a full breakdown of monthly maintenance costs for what each tier includes.

  • Premium plugins, themes, and paid tools: Priced per tool, so ask for them itemized.

  • Content and translation: Many quotes assume you supply the text and images. Bangla and English copywriting is a separate cost unless the quote says otherwise.

Yearly costs are often summarized as 10–20% of the build price. On small builds, the fixed minimums for hosting and maintenance can exceed that share.

Ongoing maintenance is the line item most cost guides skip over entirely, which is why it catches first-time buyers by surprise.


What Will Year One Really Cost? (A Worked Example)

Year one costs more than the quote. An illustrative ৳45,000 five-page brochure site from a mid-tier Dhaka agency comes to about ৳54,500 with domain and hosting, and about ৳69,500 with a basic maintenance plan, using low-to-mid points of the ranges above.

From year two, the recurring bill in this example is ৳24,500 for domain, hosting, and maintenance, and that figure drops if you skip the maintenance plan and handle updates yourself.


Realistic Budget by Business Type

A local service business typically budgets ৳18,000–৳1,50,000 for a brochure or lead-generation site, while an e-commerce store typically needs ৳1,50,000–৳5,00,000 or more. Multi-location businesses start in the lead-generation tier and rise with each location page added.

A single-location electrician and a five-location retail chain will both call their project a business website, but the second is scoped closer to a small store in complexity, even without a shopping cart.


Bangladesh vs. International Pricing: What Actually Changes

A basic Dhaka build at about 145–490 costs a fraction of typical US prices, where published guides put freelancer builds at 1,500–8,000 and agency builds at 6,000–35,000 or more. The gap reflects labor-market cost, not build quality.

US guides disagree with each other too. Business.com puts small business websites at 500–3,000, Leadpages at 500–5,000 for most small businesses, and GruffyGoat at 4,000–15,000 for a professional build. Wix places freelancer hourly rates at $50 and up.

Dhaka developers commonly bill in the range of 20–50 an hour based on current market rate patterns. A lower quote does not automatically mean lower quality, and a higher one does not automatically buy more skill. Frame Cipher is a Dhaka-based agency serving clients in Bangladesh and in the US, UK, Australia, Canada, and the UAE.


DIY or Hire Someone? A Simple Decision Framework

Choose a DIY builder for a simple brochure site on a tight budget, a freelancer for custom branding on a moderate budget, and an agency when the site needs strategy, ongoing optimization, or e-commerce and multi-location complexity. The deciding factor is who owns updates after launch.

If this describes the situation

Then this path usually fits

DIY builder

Need custom branding, moderate budget, no in-house design or development team

Solo freelancer or small studio

Need strategy, ongoing optimization, or e-commerce and multi-location complexity

Professional agency

A DIY builder puts updates on the business owner. A freelancer or agency takes that work on, at a proportionally higher price. For a deeper look at this tradeoff, see DIY builder vs. hiring a developer.

What a Fair Website Quote Should Include (Checklist)

A fair website quote itemizes the page count, design approach, platform, features and integrations, revision rounds, domain and hosting, SSL, support period, training, and ownership of files and accounts. Missing items are where cost surprises start.

  • Pages and content: How many pages, and who writes the text and supplies the images.

  • Design approach: Template or custom, and how many revision rounds are included.

  • Platform: WordPress, Webflow, or a custom build, and who can edit content afterward.

  • Features and integrations: Forms, blog, Bangla and English support, and payment gateways such as bKash and Nagad.

  • Domain, hosting, and SSL: Who buys them, what each costs per year, and whether they are registered in your name.

  • Support period: How long bug fixes are included after launch, commonly 30 days for basic builds and up to 90 days for standard builds, though this varies by provider and should always be confirmed in writing.

  • Training and handover: Whether you get a walkthrough of the content editor and the login details.

  • Payment milestones: When each installment is due and what is delivered at each stage.

Project effort on a typical build is usually weighted toward development and design, with smaller shares for discovery and testing. A quote with no design or testing line at all is worth a question.


Common Mistakes That Blow the Budget

The most common budget mistakes are underscoping the build, ignoring year-one running costs, and choosing a platform on price alone. Each tends to show up later as a rebuild or a platform migration.

  • Underscoping the initial build: Choosing the cheapest option for a business that needs lead-generation or e-commerce features, then paying to rebuild.

  • Ignoring year-one running costs: Budgeting only for the build and being surprised by hosting, renewal, and maintenance bills.

  • Choosing a platform by price alone: Picking the cheapest option without checking whether it supports the business's growth plans.

The rebuild trap is the most expensive version. For example, a ৳8,000 template site rebuilt at ৳45,000 within eighteen months costs ৳53,000 in total, more than starting with a right-sized ৳45,000 build. If the site is already live and only aging, check the signs it might be time for a redesign instead before committing to a full rebuild.


How These Prices Were Gathered

The Taka ranges in this guide reflect current market pricing patterns among Dhaka web development providers as of 2026, converted at roughly ৳123 per US dollar. International figures come from 2026 guides published by Wix, Leadpages, Business.com, and GruffyGoat.

All figures are estimates based on published pricing patterns, not a formal market survey or a guarantee of what any specific provider will quote, and individual quotes vary with scope. Prices were last checked in September 2026. For a figure tied to your own scope, request an itemized quote.

Conclusion

Three things determine what a business website costs: the build method, the type of business the site serves, and what is included after launch, not just at delivery. Budgeting for year one, including domain, hosting, and maintenance, and matching the platform to real growth plans avoids most cost surprises.

metaDescription: Compare WordPress, Webflow, and custom development on cost, speed, and scalability. A decision framework to pick the right platform for your business.
author: MD. NAHID BIN ZAMAN JOY

faqs.question: Is WordPress still worth using in 2026?
faqs.answer: Yes, for content-heavy or budget-conscious sites. WordPress remains a strong option when you manage the plugin ecosystem carefully, since unmanaged plugins are the main cause of the speed issues WordPress sites are known for.

faqs.question: Is Webflow better than WordPress for SEO?
faqs.answer: Not inherently. Both platforms can rank well in search results. The practical difference is speed and code cleanliness: Webflow outputs clean code by default, while WordPress SEO performance depends heavily on plugin choices and page-speed management.

faqs.question: How much does custom website development cost?
faqs.answer: It depends on complexity, integrations, and timeline, and it's typically the highest upfront cost of the three platforms. A simple custom-built site costs less than one with dashboards, user accounts, or third-party integrations, since each added feature requires additional development time.

faqs.question: Can a non-technical person manage a Webflow site?
faqs.answer: Yes. Webflow's visual editor is built specifically for non-developers to update content and design directly, unlike custom-coded sites, which require a developer for most changes.

faqs.question: When should a business move from WordPress to custom development?
faqs.answer: Typically, the site needs custom logic, heavy traffic handling, or integrations that no plugin supports well. This is usually a growth-stage decision rather than a starting point.

faqs.question: Does Webflow include hosting?
faqs.answer: Yes. Hosting is bundled into Webflow's plans, unlike WordPress, which requires hosting to be purchased and managed separately.

faqs.question: What's the fastest platform to launch on?
faqs.answer: WordPress and Webflow are typically both faster to launch than custom development, since both rely on templates and pre-built components rather than building every element from scratch.

content:
Picking a website platform feels like a technical decision, but it's really a business decision. The WordPress vs Webflow vs custom development question comes down to more than price; it affects who can update the site after launch, how the site performs as it grows, and how expensive it is to change your mind later.

Most comparisons stop at features: WordPress has plugins, Webflow is drag-and-drop, custom development is flexible. That's true, but it doesn't tell you which one is right for your business. This guide works through the real cost of each platform over three years, what happens if you need to switch later, and a decision framework you can apply directly to your own project.

Quick Answer: WordPress, Webflow, or Custom Development?

WordPress typically fits content-heavy sites and blogs on a limited budget, since it's free to license and has the largest plugin ecosystem for adding functionality. Webflow typically fits design-led marketing sites for teams without an in-house developer, since it bundles hosting and a visual editor into one subscription. Custom development typically fits products, dashboards, or platforms that need logic no CMS or builder can replicate, at a higher build cost and longer timeline.

Build costs generally follow that same order: WordPress sites tend to start lowest, Webflow sits in the middle once monthly plan costs are counted, and custom development carries the highest upfront investment because every component is built rather than configured.

How Each Platform Actually Works

The three platforms aren't just different tools; they're built on different mechanisms, and those mechanisms are what eventually cause problems (or don't) as a site grows.

WordPress: Runs on a content management system (CMS) that separates content from design through themes, and adds functionality through plugins. This is what makes it fast to launch; you can install a plugin instead of building a feature from scratch. It's also what causes the most common long-term issue: as more plugins get added, page speed tends to drop, since each plugin adds its own code that has to load. This directly affects Core Web Vitals, which is part of how Google evaluates page experience for search ranking.

Webflow: Uses a visual CMS where design and content structure are built directly in the browser, without writing code. Hosting is bundled into the platform itself, which removes a separate step most WordPress builds require. The tradeoff shows up as sites scale: Webflow's CMS and e-commerce plans have item limits and traffic tiers, so a site that outgrows those limits runs into a scaling ceiling that requires either a higher plan or a platform change.

Custom development: Typically built with frameworks like Next.js or React, it uses a headless architecture, where the backend that stores content is separate from the frontend that displays it.

Headless CMS: A content system where the backend (where content lives) is separated from the frontend (how it's displayed), giving developers full control over design and performance. This separation is what allows custom-built sites to load faster and scale further than most CMS or builder platforms, since there's no theme or plugin layer to work around.

This gives full control over design and logic, which is why custom development handles complex features, like user dashboards, custom integrations, or high-traffic e-commerce, that neither WordPress nor Webflow can fully replicate. The tradeoff is direct: more control means more build time and higher upfront cost, since nothing comes pre-built.

One mistake people often make here is assuming "custom" always means "better." A 5-page brochure site doesn't need headless architecture; it needs a fast, simple build, which is exactly what WordPress or Webflow already do well.

WordPress vs Webflow vs Custom Development at a Glance

The clearest way to compare all three is side by side, since the right choice usually comes down to two or three of these factors mattering more than the rest for your specific project.

WordPress and Webflow launch faster in most cases because they rely on templates and pre-built components. Custom development takes longer because there's no template to start from; every screen and interaction is designed and coded specifically for that project.

Total Cost of Ownership (3-Year View)

The upfront build price is usually the only number people compare, but it's not the number that determines whether a platform was the right choice. Hosting, plugin or app subscriptions, and ongoing maintenance all add up differently across three years, and that's where the real cost difference shows up.

This is where a lot of comparisons stop short. A WordPress site that looks cheapest at launch can end up costing more by year three if it's carrying a dozen paid plugins and needs a developer on retainer just to keep security patches current. A custom build that looks expensive upfront can end up cheaper per year once it's live, simply because there's less to maintain.


Migration & Lock-In Risk

The question almost nobody asks before choosing a platform is: what happens if this stops working for us? Each platform handles that differently, and it's worth knowing before you commit.

Moving off WordPress is usually possible, but uneven; content and images typically migrate cleanly, while custom theme code, plugin-specific functionality, and design work often don't transfer and have to be rebuilt.

Moving off Webflow means losing the native CMS structure and any Webflow-specific interactions, since that logic doesn't export to other platforms in a usable form; content generally has to be re-entered or migrated manually.

Extending a custom build later is typically the least disruptive of the three, since the codebase was built for the project specifically rather than shaped by a platform's constraints, but it does require a developer to make any changes, which WordPress and Webflow don't.

  • WordPress → elsewhere: content transfers; custom functionality usually doesn't

  • Webflow → elsewhere: CMS structure and interactions don't transfer; content re-entry is common

  • Custom → extended or rebuilt: most flexible to change, but always requires developer involvement

This usually breaks when a business picks a platform for its launch speed without asking how hard it would be to leave later. Migration is always possible; it's rarely free, and it's rarely fast.

Which One Is Right for You? (Decision Framework)

Instead of picking a platform based on which one sounds most modern, map your own project against these five variables. Most projects have a clear answer once two or three of these are weighed honestly.

  1. Budget: Tight budget and need to launch fast → WordPress or Webflow. Budget built for a long-term product → custom development.

  2. Timeline: Need to launch in a few weeks → WordPress or Webflow. Can allow 2–4 months for a build → custom development is workable.

  3. In-house skill: No developer on the team → Webflow (visual editing) or WordPress with a simple theme. Developer on staff or on retainer → custom development becomes practical to maintain.

  4. Growth trajectory: Site will likely stay a similar size and scope → WordPress or Webflow are sufficient. Expecting significant traffic growth, new features, or integrations within 1–2 years → custom development avoids a rebuild.

  5. Design complexity: Standard layouts with content variety → WordPress or Webflow templates handle this well. Highly custom interactions, dashboards, or non-standard user flows → only custom development delivers this without workarounds.

Custom development is worth the extra cost specifically when a project needs functionality, integrations, or scale that no CMS or builder can handle — not as a default choice for standard brochure or marketing sites, where it usually adds cost without adding value.

Common Mistakes When Choosing a Website Platform

The same handful of mistakes show up repeatedly, regardless of business size or industry.

  • Overbuilding: Choosing custom development for a simple 5-page brochure site, paying for flexibility that will never be used.

  • Underbuilding: Choosing WordPress or Webflow for a product that needs real custom logic, such as user accounts with complex permissions or a custom booking engine, and hitting a wall a few months in.

  • Ignoring who maintains it: Picking a platform without deciding who updates it after launch. WordPress needs regular plugin and security updates; custom development needs a developer available for changes. Skipping this conversation is one mistake people often make, and it's usually the reason a site goes stale within a year.

  • Comparing only the launch price: Choosing based on the cheapest quote without factoring in three years of hosting, plugins, and maintenance, then being surprised by the real cost later.

  • Assuming SEO is built in: All three platforms can rank well, but none of them guarantee it; technical SEO work is still required regardless of platform.

Conclusion

The right platform isn't the one with the most features; it's the one that matches your budget, your timeline, and who's actually going to maintain the site after launch. WordPress and Webflow get most standard business sites live faster and cheaper; custom development earns its higher cost only when a project needs logic or scale that no CMS or builder can provide.

Three takeaways worth remembering: total cost of ownership over three years often matters more than the upfront build price, migrating between platforms is possible but rarely simple, and choosing the first time correctly is what avoids a rebuild down the road.

If you're weighing this decision for a real project, talk to our team about your budget, timeline, and goals; we'll help you land on the platform that actually fits, not the one that's easiest to sell.

title: Shopify vs WooCommerce: Which Is Better for Your Online Store?
metaDescription: Compare Shopify and WooCommerce on cost, ease of use, and scalability. A decision framework to help you choose the right platform for your store.
author: MD. NAHID BIN ZAMAN JOY

blocks.content: Choosing between Shopify and WooCommerce website looks like a cost question on the surface, but it's really a question about who manages your store's infrastructure. The Shopify vs WooCommerce decision comes down to hosting, security, and updates: whether you want a company handling all of that for you, or whether you want full control and are willing to take on that responsibility yourself.Most comparisons stop at "Shopify costs a monthly fee, WooCommerce is free," which is misleading on both counts. This guide breaks down what each platform actually costs once transaction fees and hosting are factored in, what happens if you need to switch later, and a framework to match the right platform to your store.Quick Answer: Shopify or WooCommerce?Shopify typically fits store owners who want hosting, security, and checkout fully managed for them through one monthly subscription. WooCommerce typically fits store owners who want full control over their store and are comfortable managing, or paying someone to manage, their own WordPress hosting and plugins.Shopify's plans generally start in the tens of dollars per month and rise with higher tiers, while WooCommerce itself is free to install but requires separate hosting, security, and backup costs that vary by provider. Neither is universally cheaper; it depends on how the store is run.How Each Platform Actually WorksThe difference between Shopify and WooCommerce comes down to one core decision: hosted versus self-hosted. Everything else about cost, control, and maintenance flows from that single distinction.Hosted (SaaS) vs. Self-Hosted E-commerce Platform: A hosted platform like Shopify manages servers, security, and updates on the merchant's behalf through a monthly subscription. A self-hosted platform like WooCommerce runs on the merchant's own WordPress hosting, giving more control at the cost of more responsibility.Shopify is a hosted SaaS platform. Shopify manages the servers, security patching, and uptime, and bundles a built-in checkout into every plan. This is what makes Shopify predictable month to month: you pay a subscription, and Shopify handles the infrastructure. The tradeoff shows up at checkout: if a store uses a payment gateway other than Shopify Payments, Shopify applies a transaction fee on top of that gateway's own processing fee.WooCommerce is a free WordPress plugin that turns a WordPress site into a store, which makes it self-hosted by default. There's no bundled hosting or transaction fee layer; you choose your own hosting provider, your own payment gateway, and your own security setup. This gives full control over checkout and functionality, but it also means hosting, backups, and security updates become the store owner's responsibility (or their developer's), rather than something the platform handles automatically.One mistake people often make here is assuming "free" means WooCommerce has no real cost. WooCommerce's cost doesn't disappear; it shifts from a platform subscription to hosting, security, and plugin licenses that the owner has to manage directly.Shopify vs WooCommerce at a GlanceComparing the two side by side makes the tradeoff clearer than reading feature lists separately, since most of the differences trace back to the hosted-versus-self-hosted split.PlatformBest ForMonthly CostTransaction FeesHostingEase of UseCustomizationScalabilityShopifyStore owners who want everything managed for themSubscription-based, rises with plan tierApplies to third-party gateways; none with Shopify PaymentsBundled into the platformHigh, built for non-technical ownersGood within app/theme ecosystem, limited on checkout at lower tiersStrong, handles traffic spikes with minimal manual workWooCommerceStore owners who want full control and already use (or will manage) WordPressPlugin is free; real cost is hosting, security, and pluginsNone native to WooCommerce itselfSeparate, owner-managedModerate, benefits from WordPress familiarityVery high, full plugin and code-level controlStrong, but depends on hosting quality and server managementNeither platform is categorically cheaper; a low-traffic WooCommerce store on lean hosting can cost less than Shopify, while a WooCommerce store that needs premium hosting, security monitoring, and several paid extensions can end up costing more than a mid-tier Shopify plan.Real Cost Comparison (Transaction Fees & Hidden Costs)This is where most comparison articles fall short, and it's usually the number that actually decides the choice.Shopify charges a transaction fee on orders processed through a payment gateway other than Shopify Payments; this fee applies on top of whatever the third-party gateway itself charges, and does not apply when Shopify Payments is used as the checkout method. According to Shopify's own pricing documentation, this fee varies by plan tier, so it's worth checking current rates before comparing total cost.WooCommerce doesn't charge a native transaction fee, but that doesn't make it free. Real costs typically include:Hosting: WooCommerce needs reliable, security-hardened hosting, which carries an ongoing cost separate from the plugin itselfSecurity and backups: Not bundled in by default; usually requires a dedicated plugin or servicePremium extensions: Many features that come standard in Shopify (advanced shipping rules, subscriptions, abandoned cart recovery) require paid WooCommerce pluginsPayment gateway fees: WooCommerce doesn't add its own fee, but the connected gateway (Stripe, PayPal, etc.) still charges standard processing feesA common issue is comparing Shopify's advertised monthly price against WooCommerce's "free" plugin price without adding in what WooCommerce needs to run properly. Once hosting, security, and the extensions most stores actually need are counted, the real cost gap between the two platforms is often much smaller than it first appears.Migration & Switching ConsiderationsMoving a store between Shopify and WooCommerce is possible in both directions, but it's rarely a simple export-and-import; product data, themes, and functionality all need to be rebuilt to some degree.Moving from WooCommerce to Shopify: Product data (titles, descriptions, images, variants) typically migrates in a usable form through Shopify's import tools, but custom theme code and WooCommerce-specific plugin functionality don't transfer and have to be recreated using Shopify's app ecosystem or custom development.Moving from Shopify to WooCommerce: Product data generally exports in a workable format as well, but Shopify's checkout, app integrations, and theme design don't carry over; the store's checkout flow and design typically need to be rebuilt on WordPress.Product catalogs are the most portable piece in either directionCheckout configuration and theme design are the least portableInstalled apps/plugins almost always need direct replacements on the new platform, not a straight transferThis typically happens when a WooCommerce store outgrows its hosting, and the maintenance burden becomes too much for the team to manage, or when a Shopify store hits checkout customization limits that only a self-hosted setup can solve. Either direction is workable; it's just not instant, and it's worth budgeting real time and cost for the rebuild rather than expecting a one-click transfer.Which One Is Right for You? (Decision Framework)Instead of picking based on which platform is more talked about, weigh your store against these factors directly.Store size and catalog complexity: A small catalog with straightforward products fits either platform well. A large or highly variable catalog (bundles, subscriptions, complex variants) often runs more smoothly on WooCommerce's plugin flexibility or Shopify's higher-tier plans.Technical comfort: No developer on the team and no interest in managing hosting → Shopify. Comfortable with WordPress, or having a developer available → WooCommerce becomes practical to maintain.Budget predictability: Want one predictable monthly line item → Shopify. Comfortable managing several smaller, variable costs (hosting, plugins, security) → WooCommerce.Customization needs: Standard store layout and checkout are enough → Shopify handles this well, especially on higher plans. Need deep, non-standard checkout or functionality changes → WooCommerce's plugin and code access gives more room to work with.Order volume and growth trajectory: Expecting rapid, high-volume growth with minimal in-house technical management → Shopify's hosted infrastructure absorbs traffic spikes with less manual intervention. Steady growth with an in-house or agency dev resource → WooCommerce scales well too, as long as hosting is upgraded alongside traffic.Common Mistakes When Choosing an E-commerce PlatformThe same handful of mistakes come up repeatedly across store owners evaluating these two platforms.Comparing sticker price only: Looking at Shopify's monthly fee against WooCommerce's "free" plugin without factoring in transaction fees or hosting/security costs, then being surprised by the real total later.Underestimating WooCommerce's maintenance responsibility: Launching a WooCommerce store without a plan for who handles security updates, backups, and plugin conflicts after launch.Fighting checkout limits on lower Shopify tiers: Choosing a lower-tier Shopify plan and then needing checkout customization that tier doesn't support, forcing a plan upgrade or a platform reconsideration.Ignoring payment gateway fit: Not checking whether a preferred payment method is well-supported before committing, especially relevant for stores serving specific regions or currencies.Assuming platform choice guarantees performance: Neither platform automatically delivers fast load times or high conversion; both still require proper setup, image optimization, and app/plugin discipline.ConclusionNeither platform is better in every situation; Shopify trades control for convenience, and WooCommerce trades convenience for control. The "cheaper" option depends on real usage: transaction fees can add up on Shopify, and hosting plus premium plugins can add up just as much on WooCommerce.Three things worth remembering: the true cost of each platform only shows up once transaction fees and hosting are counted, not at the advertised price; migrating between the two is possible but requires rebuilding checkout and theme work either way; and store size, catalog complexity, and expected growth should guide the decision more than platform popularity.If you're weighing this decision for a real store, talk to our team about your catalog, budget, and growth plans; we'll help you land on the platform that actually fits your business.

faqs.question: Is Shopify worth the monthly fee?
faqs.answer: Yes, for merchants who want hosting, security, and support handled for them. The tradeoff is an ongoing subscription and, on non-Shopify Payments transactions, an added transaction fee, a cost that's worth weighing against the time saved not managing infrastructure directly.

faqs.question: Is WooCommerce really free?
faqs.answer: The plugin itself is free to install. Hosting, security, backups, and most premium extensions are not free, and together they typically make up WooCommerce's real ongoing cost.

faqs.question: Which platform is better for SEO, Shopify or WooCommerce?
faqs.answer: Both can rank well in search results. WooCommerce, through WordPress, generally offers more native content and blog SEO control, while Shopify's SEO capability depends more on theme and app choices for technical SEO flexibility.

faqs.question: Does Shopify charge transaction fees on every order?
faqs.answer: Only when a payment gateway other than Shopify Payments is used. No additional transaction fee applies when Shopify Payments is the checkout method, based on Shopify's own pricing documentation.

faqs.question: Can a non-technical person manage a Shopify store?
faqs.answer: Yes. Shopify is built for store owners without developer support, unlike WooCommerce, which typically needs ongoing technical maintenance from the owner or a developer.

faqs.question: When should a business move from WooCommerce to Shopify, or the reverse?
faqs.answer: Move to Shopify when the maintenance burden of self-hosting outweighs the value of full control. Move to WooCommerce when checkout or customization limits on Shopify become a real blocker for the business.

faqs.question: Which platform handles high order volume better?
faqs.answer: Both can scale, but Shopify's hosted infrastructure typically absorbs traffic spikes with less manual intervention than a self-managed WooCommerce and WordPress hosting setup, which depends on the hosting provider's capacity.

Shopify's plans generally start in the tens of dollars per month and rise with higher tiers, while WooCommerce itself is free to install but requires separate hosting, security, and backup costs that vary by provider. Neither is universally cheaper; it depends on how the store is run.

How Each Platform Actually Works

The difference between Shopify and WooCommerce comes down to one core decision: hosted versus self-hosted. Everything else about cost, control, and maintenance flows from that single distinction.

Hosted (SaaS) vs. Self-Hosted E-commerce Platform: A hosted platform like Shopify manages servers, security, and updates on the merchant's behalf through a monthly subscription. A self-hosted platform like WooCommerce runs on the merchant's own WordPress hosting, giving more control at the cost of more responsibility.


Shopify is a hosted SaaS platform. Shopify manages the servers, security patching, and uptime, and bundles a built-in checkout into every plan. This is what makes Shopify predictable month to month: you pay a subscription, and Shopify handles the infrastructure. The tradeoff shows up at checkout: if a store uses a payment gateway other than Shopify Payments, Shopify applies a transaction fee on top of that gateway's own processing fee.

WooCommerce is a free WordPress plugin that turns a WordPress site into a store, which makes it self-hosted by default. There's no bundled hosting or transaction fee layer; you choose your own hosting provider, your own payment gateway, and your own security setup. This gives full control over checkout and functionality, but it also means hosting, backups, and security updates become the store owner's responsibility (or their developer's), rather than something the platform handles automatically.

One mistake people often make here is assuming "free" means WooCommerce has no real cost. WooCommerce's cost doesn't disappear; it shifts from a platform subscription to hosting, security, and plugin licenses that the owner has to manage directly.

Shopify vs WooCommerce at a Glance

Comparing the two side by side makes the tradeoff clearer than reading feature lists separately, since most of the differences trace back to the hosted-versus-self-hosted split.

Neither platform is categorically cheaper; a low-traffic WooCommerce store on lean hosting can cost less than Shopify, while a WooCommerce store that needs premium hosting, security monitoring, and several paid extensions can end up costing more than a mid-tier Shopify plan.


Real Cost Comparison (Transaction Fees & Hidden Costs)

This is where most comparison articles fall short, and it's usually the number that actually decides the choice.

Shopify charges a transaction fee on orders processed through a payment gateway other than Shopify Payments; this fee applies on top of whatever the third-party gateway itself charges, and does not apply when Shopify Payments is used as the checkout method. According to Shopify's own pricing documentation, this fee varies by plan tier, so it's worth checking current rates before comparing total cost.

WooCommerce doesn't charge a native transaction fee, but that doesn't make it free. Real costs typically include:

  • Hosting: WooCommerce needs reliable, security-hardened hosting, which carries an ongoing cost separate from the plugin itself

  • Security and backups: Not bundled in by default; usually requires a dedicated plugin or service

  • Premium extensions: Many features that come standard in Shopify (advanced shipping rules, subscriptions, abandoned cart recovery) require paid WooCommerce plugins

  • Payment gateway fees: WooCommerce doesn't add its own fee, but the connected gateway (Stripe, PayPal, etc.) still charges standard processing fees

A common issue is comparing Shopify's advertised monthly price against WooCommerce's "free" plugin price without adding in what WooCommerce needs to run properly. Once hosting, security, and the extensions most stores actually need are counted, the real cost gap between the two platforms is often much smaller than it first appears.

Migration & Switching Considerations

Moving a store between Shopify and WooCommerce is possible in both directions, but it's rarely a simple export-and-import; product data, themes, and functionality all need to be rebuilt to some degree.

Moving from WooCommerce to Shopify: Product data (titles, descriptions, images, variants) typically migrates in a usable form through Shopify's import tools, but custom theme code and WooCommerce-specific plugin functionality don't transfer and have to be recreated using Shopify's app ecosystem or custom development.

Moving from Shopify to WooCommerce: Product data generally exports in a workable format as well, but Shopify's checkout, app integrations, and theme design don't carry over; the store's checkout flow and design typically need to be rebuilt on WordPress.

  • Product catalogs are the most portable piece in either direction

  • Checkout configuration and theme design are the least portable

  • Installed apps/plugins almost always need direct replacements on the new platform, not a straight transfer

This typically happens when a WooCommerce store outgrows its hosting, and the maintenance burden becomes too much for the team to manage, or when a Shopify store hits checkout customization limits that only a self-hosted setup can solve. Either direction is workable; it's just not instant, and it's worth budgeting real time and cost for the rebuild rather than expecting a one-click transfer.

Which One Is Right for You? (Decision Framework)

Instead of picking based on which platform is more talked about, weigh your store against these factors directly.

  1. Store size and catalog complexity: A small catalog with straightforward products fits either platform well. A large or highly variable catalog (bundles, subscriptions, complex variants) often runs more smoothly on WooCommerce's plugin flexibility or Shopify's higher-tier plans.

  2. Technical comfort: No developer on the team and no interest in managing hosting → Shopify. Comfortable with WordPress, or having a developer available → WooCommerce becomes practical to maintain.

  3. Budget predictability: Want one predictable monthly line item → Shopify. Comfortable managing several smaller, variable costs (hosting, plugins, security) → WooCommerce.

  4. Customization needs: Standard store layout and checkout are enough → Shopify handles this well, especially on higher plans. Need deep, non-standard checkout or functionality changes → WooCommerce's plugin and code access gives more room to work with.

  5. Order volume and growth trajectory: Expecting rapid, high-volume growth with minimal in-house technical management → Shopify's hosted infrastructure absorbs traffic spikes with less manual intervention. Steady growth with an in-house or agency dev resource → WooCommerce scales well too, as long as hosting is upgraded alongside traffic.

Common Mistakes When Choosing an E-commerce Platform

The same handful of mistakes come up repeatedly across store owners evaluating these two platforms.

  • Comparing sticker price only: Looking at Shopify's monthly fee against WooCommerce's "free" plugin without factoring in transaction fees or hosting/security costs, then being surprised by the real total later.

  • Underestimating WooCommerce's maintenance responsibility: Launching a WooCommerce store without a plan for who handles security updates, backups, and plugin conflicts after launch.

  • Fighting checkout limits on lower Shopify tiers: Choosing a lower-tier Shopify plan and then needing checkout customization that tier doesn't support, forcing a plan upgrade or a platform reconsideration.

  • Ignoring payment gateway fit: Not checking whether a preferred payment method is well-supported before committing, especially relevant for stores serving specific regions or currencies.

  • Assuming platform choice guarantees performance: Neither platform automatically delivers fast load times or high conversion; both still require proper setup, image optimization, and app/plugin discipline.

Conclusion

Neither platform is better in every situation; Shopify trades control for convenience, and WooCommerce trades convenience for control. The "cheaper" option depends on real usage: transaction fees can add up on Shopify, and hosting plus premium plugins can add up just as much on WooCommerce.

Three things worth remembering: the true cost of each platform only shows up once transaction fees and hosting are counted, not at the advertised price; migrating between the two is possible but requires rebuilding checkout and theme work either way; and store size, catalog complexity, and expected growth should guide the decision more than platform popularity.

If you're weighing this decision for a real store, talk to our team about your catalog, budget, and growth plans; we'll help you land on the platform that actually fits your business.

faqs.question: How do I know if my website is outdated?
faqs.answer: Compare it against the 7 signs above; a site showing 2 or more, especially the revenue-impacting ones like poor mobile usability or low conversion despite good traffic, is a reasonably strong signal it's time for a redesign.

faqs.question: How much does a website redesign cost?
faqs.answer: It depends heavily on scope; a visual refresh within the existing structure costs far less than a full rebuild with a new CMS or added functionality. Getting a specific quote requires defining which of the 7 signs apply to your site first.

faqs.question: How often should a business redesign its website?
faqs.answer: There's no fixed schedule. Redesign timing should be triggered by the signs in this article, bounce rate trends, conversion data, and maintainability, rather than a calendar interval like "every 3 years."

faqs.question: Can I fix these issues without a full redesign?
faqs.answer: Some signs, like slow page speed, can sometimes be fixed without a full redesign through hosting or image optimization. Others, like outdated branding or a CMS that's become difficult to maintain, usually can't be solved without a structural rebuild.

faqs.question: What's the difference between a website redesign and a website refresh?
faqs.answer: A refresh typically updates visuals or content within the existing site structure: new images, updated copy, minor style changes. A redesign typically changes the structure, user experience, and often the underlying platform itself.

faqs.question: Does a redesign guarantee better conversions?
faqs.answer: No. A redesign improves the conditions for better conversion, clearer navigation, faster load times, and a stronger conversion path, but actual results still depend on execution, the offer itself, and ongoing optimization after launch.

content:
Most businesses don't redesign their website. They plan to redesign it because something started feeling off, and they couldn't tell if it was a real problem or just impatience. These 7 signs your website needs a redesign are meant to replace that guessing with an actual self-check, so you know whether the issue is design or something else being misdiagnosed as design.

Of the redesign projects taken on in a typical year, the most commonly cited starting reason clients give is rarely "I want a new look", it's usually a symptom like low conversions or a site that's become hard to update, with the visual outdatedness noticed only after that. That distinction matters, because redesigning for the wrong reason often fixes the appearance without fixing the actual problem.

Quick Answer: The 7 Signs Your Website Needs a Redesign

The clearest signs a website needs a redesign are: a high and rising bounce rate, a mobile experience that's technically responsive but not actually usable, navigation visitors can't find their way through, page speed that's working against you, branding that no longer matches the business, a conversion rate that doesn't match your traffic, and a site that feels difficult or risky to update.

Website Redesign: A structural and visual overhaul of a site's design, user experience, and often its underlying code or content management system. This is distinct from smaller updates like a content refresh, a new page, or a minor style tweak, which don't require rebuilding the site's structure.

Each sign below includes a short self-check and a note on whether it's typically a cosmetic issue or one that's actively costing revenue.

Sign 1: Your Bounce Rate Is High and Rising

A bounce rate that's climbing, especially on pages that used to hold attention, usually points to a first-impression problem: visitors land, don't see what they expect within a few seconds, and leave.

There's no single "good" bounce rate that applies across every industry or page type, so the more useful check is the trend: has it gone up over the last 3–6 months without a change in your traffic sources? If yes, that's a stronger signal than the raw number itself.

Self-check: In Google Analytics, compare your bounce rate for the same pages over two periods 3–6 months apart. If it's risen noticeably and your traffic sources haven't changed, the page itself is likely the problem.

A mistake people often make here is assuming any high bounce rate is a design issue. If the traffic bringing people to the page doesn't match what the page actually offers- for example, an ad or search result promising something the page doesn't deliver- that's a targeting or content mismatch, not a redesign problem.

Sign 2: Your Site Isn't Mobile-Friendly (or Just Barely Is)

A site that passes a basic responsiveness test can still fail visitors in practice: buttons too small to tap accurately, text that requires zooming, or forms that are painful to fill out on a phone.

"Technically responsive" and "actually usable on mobile" are different things. Most sites resize correctly across screen widths but still create friction once someone tries to actually use the site with their thumb instead of a mouse.

Self-check: Open your site on an actual phone (not a browser's device-resize tool) and try to complete your site's main action, filling a contact form, adding a product to cart, or booking a service. If it takes noticeably more effort than it should, that's the sign showing up in practice.

This is often the highest-impact sign on this list, since mobile traffic frequently makes up the majority of visits for many businesses, and a broken mobile experience affects that majority directly.

Sign 3: Visitors Can't Find What They're Looking For

When visitors land on a site and can't quickly find the page or information they need, they typically don't dig; they leave and try a competitor instead.

This usually shows up as a navigation or information architecture problem: too many menu items, unclear labels, or important pages buried more than two clicks deep.

Self-check: Check Google Search Console for queries where your site ranks but gets low click-through, or review your site's internal search data (if available) for repeated searches that don't match your main navigation labels; both point to a mismatch between what visitors expect and what your navigation offers.

A better way to think about this than "the menu needs updating" is to ask whether a first-time visitor could find your three most important pages in under 10 seconds. If not, the navigation structure is working against the business, not just looking dated.

Sign 4: Your Page Speed Is Working Against You

Slow page speed hurts in two ways at once: visitors leave before the page finishes loading, and search engines factor load speed into ranking through Core Web Vitals.

According to Google's Core Web Vitals documentation, Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) should occur within 2.5 seconds of when the page starts loading for a good user experience. Pages that consistently miss this threshold are working against both user experience and search visibility at the same time.

Self-check: Run your homepage and one or two key landing pages through Google PageSpeed Insights and note the Core Web Vitals scores, particularly LCP.

This depends on the cause, though; slow speed is sometimes a hosting or image-optimization problem rather than a full redesign issue. Before committing to a rebuild, it's worth ruling out compressed images, a faster host, or caching as a lower-cost fix first.

Sign 5: Your Brand Has Evolved, but Your Website Hasn't

A business that has changed its positioning, pricing tier, or core offering since the site was built often ends up with a website that quietly contradicts what the business actually is now.

This is the sign most often dismissed as "just cosmetic," but a visual identity that doesn't match the current business directly affects how credible and current the business looks to a new visitor comparing options.

Self-check: Look at your homepage as if you were a new visitor with no history with the business. Does it accurately represent who you serve and what you offer today, or does it describe an earlier version of the business?

The practical difference between this sign and outdated design trends alone is that this one is about accuracy, not aesthetics; a site can look reasonably current and still misrepresent the business.

Sign 6: Your Conversion Rate Doesn't Match Your Traffic

Healthy traffic with disappointing conversions usually means the problem isn't attracting visitors; it's what happens once they arrive.

This is the clearest revenue-impacting sign on this list, since it directly measures lost business rather than a proxy metric like bounce rate or session time.

Self-check: Compare your conversion rate on mobile versus desktop, and check whether your primary call-to-action is visible without scrolling on your most-visited landing pages. A meaningful gap between mobile and desktop conversion, or a buried call-to-action, usually explains part of the shortfall.

What matters most here is not assuming this is automatically a marketing problem. If the traffic is qualified (the right audience, from the right channels) and conversion is still low, the conversion path itself- page layout, form length, trust signals- is the more likely cause.

Sign 7: Updating Your Website Feels Difficult or Risky

A site that nobody on the team feels confident editing, where a small text change requires a developer, or where updates sometimes break something else, has become an operational liability, not just an aesthetic one.

This typically happens with older custom-coded sites, heavily customized CMS installs, or platforms the original developer no longer supports. It's rarely covered in generic redesign checklists, which tend to focus on what a visitor sees rather than what the business experiences behind the scenes.

Self-check: Ask whoever manages the site day-to-day how confident they feel making a routine update of a new page, a price change, a blog post, without help. Hesitation or "we usually wait and batch changes" is a sign the underlying platform has become a constraint.

This sign is often the real trigger behind a redesign decision even when the stated reason given is something else, since a site that's painful to maintain tends to get neglected, which compounds the other six signs over time.

Which Signs Are Cosmetic vs Revenue-Impacting?

Not every sign on this list carries the same urgency; some affect how the site looks, others affect how much revenue it's costing you right now.

Reading this table alongside the 7 signs above gives a fast way to decide which issues to prioritize first, rather than treating all of them as equally urgent.


What to Check Before You Commit to a Redesign

Before booking a full redesign, it's worth confirming the real cause isn't something smaller and cheaper to fix.

  • Rule out hosting and page speed first; a slow host or unoptimized images can look like a design problem but may only need a hosting upgrade or image compression.

  • Check your tracking setup: if Google Analytics or conversion tracking isn't set up correctly, the data you're using to diagnose the site could be misleading you.

  • Separate traffic quality from site performance; a high bounce rate from mismatched ad targeting is a marketing fix, not a design fix.

  • Confirm it's not a content or SEO issue; declining organic traffic despite steady content output often points to SEO or content strategy, not the site's design.

  • Get a second opinion before rebuilding; a short audit from a developer or agency can confirm whether the issue is structural (needs a redesign) or fixable within the current site.

This usually breaks when businesses jump straight to "we need a new website" based on a feeling rather than checking these first. Sometimes that's the right call, but often a smaller, targeted fix solves the actual problem for a fraction of the cost.

Conclusion

Not every sign on this list requires a full redesign on its own; some, like slow page speed, are worth checking as a smaller fix first before assuming the whole site needs to be rebuilt.

The signs that affect revenue directly, like a mismatched conversion rate or a broken mobile experience, deserve more urgency than the purely cosmetic ones like outdated branding. A redesign decision should be triggered by evidence, bounce rate trends, conversion data, or a CMS that's become an operational liability, not by how the site subjectively "feels" to look at.

If two or more of these signs sound familiar, talk to our team about a quick audit of your site; we'll help you confirm whether it's a redesign issue or something smaller and less expensive to fix first.

seoTitle: What Is a Landing Page? How Is It Different From a Website
title: What Is a Landing Page? How Is It Different From a Website
metaDescription: Learn what a landing page actually is, how it differs from a website, and when to use each, with a clear comparison and real examples.
author: MD. NAHID BIN ZAMAN JOY

faqs.question: Is a homepage a landing page?
faqs.answer: Generally not. Homepages usually include navigation and serve multiple purposes at once, while a landing page is built around a single conversion goal with no navigation to distract from it.

faqs.question: Do I need a landing page if I already have a website?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes, if you're running paid campaigns. A website and a landing page typically serve different purposes, and most businesses running paid ads benefit from having both rather than relying on the website alone.

faqs.question: Can a landing page replace a website?
faqs.answer: No. A landing page is built for one conversion goal and lacks the navigation and content depth a business website needs to support general visibility, multiple offerings, and organic search traffic.

faqs.question: Why don't landing pages have navigation menus?
faqs.answer: Navigation is intentionally removed to keep visitor attention on the single conversion goal. Without a menu to click away to, visitors are more likely to complete the one action the page is asking for.

faqs.question: What's an example of when to use a landing page?
faqs.answer: Paid ad campaigns, lead-generation offers like ebooks or webinars, and single-promotion pages (like a limited-time discount) are common landing page use cases, since each has one clear, specific goal.

faqs.question: Does a landing page help or hurt SEO?
faqs.answer: Landing pages can be indexed and found in search, but they're usually built for conversion rather than organic ranking. This means they typically play a different role than core website content in an overall SEO strategy, rather than competing with it directly.

content:
A landing page and a website page look similar but are built to do completely different jobs, and mixing them up is one of the most common reasons ad campaigns underperform. What is a landing page versus a website page is one of the most commonly confused distinctions in digital marketing, and the confusion isn't just semantic; it directly affects campaign performance.

The short version: a landing page and a regular website page look similar but are built for completely different jobs. Getting this distinction right before your next campaign, launch, or ad spend can be the difference between a page that converts and one that just sits there.

What Is a Landing Page?

call to actionA landing page is a standalone web page built for a single, specific purpose, usually to convert visitors arriving from a targeted campaign, such as a paid ad, an email, or a social post. Unlike a regular website page, a landing page typically has no navigation menu, no links to other pages, and one clear call to action.

Landing Page: A standalone web page built for a single, specific purpose, usually to convert visitors arriving from a targeted campaign, distinguished from a regular website page by having a single conversion goal and typically no navigation menu.

Everything about a landing page's structure exists to support that one goal. There's no "About" link to click, no blog to browse, nothing to distract from the one action it's asking the visitor to take.

How a Landing Page Differs From a Website

The core difference between a landing page and a website comes down to how many goals each one is trying to accomplish, and that single distinction explains almost every structural difference between the two.

A landing page is built around a single conversion goal: signing up for a webinar, downloading a guide, and claiming a discount. Because that one goal is the entire point of the page, the navigation menu is intentionally removed. Without a menu to click away to, visitor attention stays focused on the one call to action, which is what makes a well-built landing page convert at a higher rate for that specific action than a general page would.

A website, by contrast, is built around multiple pages and multiple goals, informing visitors about your services, building trust through an About page, answering questions, and eventually guiding different visitors toward different next steps. This is why a website needs a navigation menu: visitors are expected to explore, not just complete one action and leave.

One mistake people often make is assuming a landing page is just "a website with fewer pages." The difference isn't page count but its purpose. A landing page could technically be part of a larger website's domain and still function as a true landing page, as long as it keeps that single-goal, no-navigation structure.

Landing Page vs Website Page: Key Differences

Seeing the two side by side makes the distinction concrete, especially for anyone deciding which one to build next.

Attribute

Landing Page

Website Page

Purpose

One specific conversion action

Multiple goals: inform, build trust, support navigation

Navigation

Typically none

Full site navigation menu

Typical Traffic Source

Paid ads, email campaigns, social posts

Organic search, direct visits, internal links

Conversion Goal

Single, focused call to action

Varies by page; often multiple paths

Typical Use Case

Campaign, promotion, lead-generation offer

General business presence, ongoing content

A page missing most of these landing-page traits full navigation, multiple links, several competing calls to action is functioning as a website page, even if it was technically built to receive campaign traffic.

Is a Homepage a Landing Page?

A homepage is generally not a landing page, even though visitors technically "land" on it. The reason comes down to purpose and structure, not just terminology.

Most homepages include full navigation, link out to services, About, and Contact pages, and try to serve many different visitor intents at once: someone comparing options, someone researching, someone ready to buy. That's the opposite of a landing page's single-goal design.

This is the most common real-world mix-up in this topic, and it's rarely addressed directly: marketers sometimes send paid ad traffic straight to the homepage because it's already built and "technically a page visitors land on." The homepage's navigation and competing messages then work against the ad's specific offer, diluting the one action the campaign was trying to drive.

A homepage can share some surface similarities with a landing page; both can be a single page a visitor arrives at directly, but a true landing page is defined by removing everything that isn't the one conversion goal, which a homepage, by design, doesn't do.

When to Use a Landing Page vs a Website

Most businesses don't need to choose one over the other; a landing page and a website typically serve different, complementary roles, and using them together is usually the right approach.

Use a landing page when:

  • Running a paid ad campaign (Google Ads, Meta Ads) with one specific offer

  • Promoting a single event, webinar, or limited-time discount

  • Collecting leads through a gated resource like an ebook or guide

  • Testing a specific message or offer through A/B testing before committing to it site-wide

Use a website when:

  • Building general brand visibility and credibility

  • Showcasing multiple services, products, or offerings

  • Supporting organic search traffic across many different topics and queries

  • Giving visitors the ability to explore and self-select their own next step

A better way to think about this than "landing page or website" is: the landing page supports a specific campaign's one goal, while the website supports everything else about the business's ongoing presence. Most active marketing efforts end up needing both working together rather than one replacing the other.

Common Mistakes When Using Landing Pages and Websites

A handful of mistakes show up repeatedly once businesses start running campaigns without a clear landing page strategy.

  • Sending paid ad traffic to the homepage instead of a dedicated landing page: This typically lowers conversion rate, since the homepage's navigation and multiple messages compete with the ad's specific offer instead of reinforcing it.

  • Adding full site navigation to a landing page: This defeats the page's purpose by giving visitors an easy way to click away before completing the one action the page was built for.

  • Treating a landing page as a substitute for a full website: A landing page isn't built for organic visibility, content depth, or multiple visitor intents, so it can't replace a real website's role in the business.

  • Mismatched messaging between the ad and the landing page: If the headline or offer on the landing page doesn't clearly match what the ad promised, visitors often leave immediately, regardless of how well-designed the page is.

A common issue tied to the first mistake above is a drop in ad relevance or Quality Score when traffic is sent somewhere that doesn't match the ad's intent, something worth checking directly in your ad platform's own guidelines if paid campaigns are involved.

Conclusion

A landing page and a website aren't competing tools; they're built for different jobs. A landing page is defined by its single conversion goal and lack of navigation, not simply by being "one page," and a homepage generally doesn't qualify as a landing page even though visitors can land on it directly.

Most businesses running paid campaigns need both: a website for ongoing visibility and multiple visitor journeys, and dedicated landing pages for each specific campaign or offer. Getting this right before your next ad spend is one of the simplest ways to protect your conversion rate.

If you're planning a campaign and aren't sure whether you need a landing page, a website update, or both, talk to our team; we'll help you figure out which one actually fits what you're trying to achieve.

faqs.question: How often should a website be maintained?
faqs.answer: Certain tasks, security updates, backups, uptime, and functionality checks, should happen monthly, while others, like deep audits or a full design review, can happen quarterly or annually without added risk.

faqs.question: What happens if I don't maintain my website?
faqs.answer: Skipped maintenance typically leads to security vulnerabilities, performance decline, broken functionality, or silent tracking failures. These problems tend to compound the longer they go unnoticed, since small issues become harder to fix the longer they're left alone.

faqs.question: Can I do website maintenance myself?
faqs.answer: Some tasks, form testing, broken link checks, analytics review, don't require technical skill and can be done by anyone comfortable navigating the site. Others, like plugin and CMS updates or security fixes, are safer handled by a developer or maintenance provider, since a failed update can take a site offline.

faqs.question: How much does website maintenance cost?
faqs.answer: It depends on scope, whether maintenance is handled in-house with occasional developer support or through an ongoing maintenance retainer with an agency. The right approach usually depends on how much of this checklist a team can realistically manage monthly on its own.

faqs.question: What's the difference between website maintenance and a website redesign?
faqs.answer: Maintenance is ongoing upkeep to keep an existing site secure and functional. A redesign is a structural overhaul of the site's design and user experience, typically triggered by different signs entirely, such as declining conversion rates or an outdated visual identity.

faqs.question: How do I know if my website has a security vulnerability?
faqs.answer: Outdated plugin or CMS versions, unexpected site behavior, or flags from a security scan or hosting provider are common indicators, and checking for these directly is exactly what the monthly security check on this list is for.
