faqs.question: How long does a technical SEO audit take?
faqs.answer: It depends on site size and complexity. A small site can often be reviewed in a few hours, while large or JavaScript-heavy sites take longer because of more templates, more URLs, and more rendering checks. Fixing the issues usually takes longer than finding them.

faqs.question: Can I do a technical SEO audit for free?
faqs.answer: Yes. Google Search Console, PageSpeed Insights, Lighthouse, Chrome DevTools, and the free version of Screaming Frog cover most checks. The main limit is crawl size, since free crawlers cap how many URLs they scan, so large sites may need sampling or a paid tool.

faqs.question: How often should I run a technical SEO audit?
faqs.answer: Run one after major changes such as a migration, redesign, or platform switch, and on a recurring schedule suited to your site’s size and update frequency. Larger, fast-changing sites typically need more frequent checks. No single interval fits every website.

faqs.question: What is the most important thing to check first?
faqs.answer: Check whether your important pages are indexable and actually indexed. If Google cannot crawl or index a page, no other optimization matters for that page. Start with the Page indexing report in Search Console and look for noindex tags and robots.txt blocks.

faqs.question: What’s the difference between a technical SEO audit and a full SEO audit?
faqs.answer: A technical SEO audit covers infrastructure: crawling, indexing, rendering, speed, security, and structured data. A full SEO audit adds content quality, on-page optimization, keyword targeting, and backlinks. The technical audit is typically the first layer, because content cannot rank if pages can’t be indexed.

faqs.question: Do I need a developer to fix audit issues?
faqs.answer: Often, yes, for redirects, server errors, speed, and rendering problems. Many other fixes, such as sitemaps, internal links, titles, noindex tags, and canonicals, can usually be handled in your CMS or an SEO plugin. The answer depends on your platform and how much of your code you control.

faqs.question: Does a technical SEO audit help with AI search visibility?
faqs.answer: It can help. AI search features generally draw on pages that search engines can crawl, index, and understand, so indexability and clear structure are the starting point. A technical audit improves those conditions, but it does not guarantee a page will be cited or shown.

blocks.content: You published the pages, tuned the keywords, and still nothing shows up in search. Often the problem isn’t the content. Google may be unable to crawl a page, may choose not to index it, or may see something different from what visitors see.Learning how to do a technical SEO audit gives you a repeatable way to find those problems using free tools and a fixed order of checks. This guide covers ten steps, each with a pass criterion, a severity level, and the tool that checks it. The quick answer comes first.How to Do a Technical SEO Audit: Quick AnswerTo do a technical SEO audit, crawl your site, check which pages Google has indexed, review robots.txt and sitemaps, fix status codes and redirects, resolve canonical conflicts, review internal links, test mobile rendering, measure Core Web Vitals, check HTTPS, and validate structured data, in that order.Definition: Technical SEO audit A technical SEO audit is a systematic review of a website’s crawlability, indexability, rendering, structure, security, and performance, designed to find the issues that stop search engines from discovering, understanding, and ranking its pages.The ten steps in order:Crawl your website to build a URL inventory.Check which pages Google has indexed in Search Console.Audit robots.txt and XML sitemaps for access and discovery problems.Fix status codes, redirects, and broken links.Resolve canonical and duplicate URL issues.Review site structure, internal links, and orphan pages.Test mobile usability and JavaScript rendering.Measure Core Web Vitals and page speed.Check HTTPS and website security.Validate structured data.The order follows how Google processes a site: it crawls a URL, indexes it, renders it, and then ranks it. A page that cannot be crawled cannot be indexed, and a page that cannot be indexed gains nothing from speed or schema fixes. That is why indexing checks come before performance checks.What You Need Before You Start: Free Audit ToolsA free technical SEO audit needs Google Search Console, PageSpeed Insights, Lighthouse, Chrome DevTools, a free crawler such as the free version of Screaming Frog SEO Spider, and optionally Ahrefs Webmaster Tools. Together they cover indexing, site-wide status data, rendering, and performance.ToolWhat it checksFree limitsGoogle Search ConsoleIndexing status, robots.txt report, sitemaps, Core Web Vitals field data, security issuesFree; requires verifying site ownershipPageSpeed InsightsCore Web Vitals field data (when available) and lab diagnosticsFree; one URL at a timeLighthouseLab data for performance, accessibility, and SEO basicsFree; built into Chrome DevToolsChrome DevToolsRendered HTML, network requests, mobile emulationFree; built into ChromeScreaming Frog SEO SpiderStatus codes, canonicals, titles, headings, crawl depth, broken linksFree version crawls up to 500 URLs, per the vendor’s documentationAhrefs Webmaster ToolsSite audit and backlink data for sites you ownFree for verified sitesGoogle Analytics 4Landing pages that receive trafficFreeWhen choosing tools, ask two questions. Does the tool use Google’s own data? Does it show page-level detail you can act on?A crawler shows what could be wrong, while Search Console shows what Google actually sees. One mistake people often make is trusting a crawler report alone. The audit needs both, because a crawler cannot tell you which URLs Google has chosen to index.Before starting, verify your site in Search Console and confirm GA4 is collecting data. Without verification, the indexing and Core Web Vitals checks later in the audit are not available.Step 1: Crawl Your WebsiteA site crawl is an automated scan that follows links from your homepage and records each URL’s status code, title, canonical, indexability, and depth. In an audit, the crawl produces the URL inventory that every later step checks against.Open your crawler and enter your homepage URL, using the full https:// version.Add your sitemap if the tool allows it, so pages with no internal links are included.Run the crawl and wait for it to finish. On large sites, a free crawler may stop at its URL cap.Export the key columns: URL, status code, indexability, canonical, title, and crawl depth.Save the export as your baseline. You will re-crawl later to confirm fixes worked.On a large site, sample by page template instead of by URL count. Check one page each from the homepage, category, blog post, and product templates. One broken template can affect thousands of pages, so a single fix at the template level often resolves them all.A common mistake is crawling only the homepage and a few links, then treating the result as the whole site. If the crawl hits a limit, note which templates it did not reach.Step 2: Check Which Pages Google Has IndexedTo check whether pages are indexed, open the Page indexing report in Google Search Console, review the indexed and not-indexed totals, and then run URL Inspection on individual pages. Compare Google’s indexed list against the indexable URLs from your crawl to find gaps.StatusWhat it meansNext actionCrawled – currently not indexedGoogle fetched the page but chose not to index itReview content quality and uniqueness; check for duplicatesDiscovered – currently not indexedGoogle knows the URL but has not crawled it yetAdd internal links; confirm it is in the sitemapExcluded by ‘noindex’ tagThe page tells Google not to index itRemove the tag if the page should rankBlocked by robots.txtGoogle is not allowed to crawl the URLEdit robots.txt if the page should be crawledDuplicate, Google chose a different canonicalGoogle picked another URL as the main versionAlign canonicals, redirects, and internal linksPage with redirectThe URL redirects elsewhereUsually fine; make sure internal links point to the final URLThe most damaging edge case is a noindex tag left on after launch. A staging setting carries into production, and important pages quietly drop out of search while the team keeps publishing.“Crawled – currently not indexed” is often a content-quality signal rather than a technical bug. Google may judge the page thin, repetitive, or too similar to another page. Fixing it usually means improving the page, not editing code.To compare lists, export your crawl’s indexable URLs and the indexed URLs from Search Console. Pages in the first list but missing from the second are your investigation queue.Step 3: Audit Robots.txt and XML SitemapsCheck that robots.txt does not block important pages or CSS and JavaScript files, and that your XML sitemap lists only canonical, indexable URLs that return a 200 status. Robots.txt controls crawl access, while the sitemap helps search engines discover pages.Robots.txtLook for accidental disallows. A Disallow: / copied from a staging site blocks the entire site.Check for blocked resources. Blocking CSS or JavaScript files can stop Google from rendering pages correctly.Use the robots.txt report in Search Console to confirm Google can fetch and parse the file.Keep the file small. According to Google’s documentation, Google processes only the first 500 KiB of a robots.txt file.XML sitemapsList only indexable URLs. Remove redirected, noindexed, canonicalized, and error URLs.Respect the limits. Per Google Search Central documentation, one sitemap file can hold up to 50,000 URLs or 50 MB uncompressed. Larger sites use a sitemap index.Submit the sitemap in Search Console and check for errors.Keep lastmod honest. Update it only when page content changes.A noindex tag and a robots.txt block conflict with each other. Google cannot see a noindex tag on a page it is not allowed to crawl, so the URL may stay in the index. To remove a page from search, allow crawling and use noindex.Step 4: Fix Status Codes, Redirects, and Broken LinksThe HTTP status codes that matter most in a technical SEO audit are 200 (OK), 301 (permanent redirect), 302 (temporary redirect), 404 (not found), 410 (gone), and 5xx (server errors). Each tells search engines how to treat a URL, and 5xx errors are the most urgent.CodeMeaningAction200Page loads normallyNo action; confirm it is the intended URL301Permanent redirectFine when pointing to the correct final URL302Temporary redirectChange to 301 if the move is permanent404Page not foundFix only if the page has links, traffic, or a replacement410Permanently removedUse for pages you deliberately deleted5xxServer errorFix immediately; check hosting and server logsRedirect chains happen when one URL redirects to another that redirects again. Loops send crawlers in circles. Per Google’s documentation, Googlebot follows up to 10 redirect hops, but shorter chains are faster and safer. Aim for one hop from the old URL to the final one.A soft 404 is a page that shows “not found” content but returns a 200 status. Search Console reports these, and the fix is to return a real 404 or restore the content.Update internal links to point to the final URL instead of relying on redirects. Redirects are a safety net, not a substitute for correct links.Not every 404 needs fixing. According to Google’s guidance, 404 errors on URLs that never existed or have no value do not harm the rest of your site. Prioritize broken URLs that have backlinks, internal links, or traffic.Step 5: Resolve Canonical and Duplicate URL IssuesA canonical tag is an HTML element that tells search engines which URL is the preferred version when the same or very similar content exists at several addresses. It consolidates ranking signals onto one URL and reduces duplicate indexing.Common causes of duplicate URLs:www vs non-www: www.example.com and example.com both load.HTTP vs HTTPS: both versions return a page.Trailing slashes: /shoes and /shoes/ serve the same content.URL parameters: filters, sorting, and tracking codes create new URLs.A mini example: if example.com/shoes?color=red shows a filtered view of the main shoes page, its canonical tag should point to example.com/shoes. The main page should carry a self-referencing canonical that points to itself.Google treats canonicals as a hint, not a command. When signals conflict, such as a canonical pointing one way, a redirect another, and the sitemap listing a third URL, Google may choose a different URL than you intended. Search Console reports this as “Duplicate, Google chose different canonical than user.”Teams often run into this after a migration, when old canonicals are copied across. The fix is consistency: the canonical, internal links, redirects, and sitemap should all name the same URL.Step 6: Review Site Structure, Internal Links, and Orphan PagesAn orphan page is a page with no internal links pointing to it, which makes it hard for search engines to discover and weakens its authority. To find one, compare the URLs in your sitemap and GA4 landing pages against the URLs your crawler reached through links.Check crawl depth. Pages many clicks from the homepage are typically discovered and revisited less reliably. Google publishes no fixed depth limit, so use depth as a relative signal and look for important pages buried deeper than they should be.Find orphan pages. Pages in the sitemap or in GA4 landing page reports that your crawl did not reach through links are orphan candidates.Check hub and cluster links. Each main topic page should link to its supporting articles, and those articles should link back.Review anchor text. Descriptive anchors tell search engines what the target page is about. Anchors like “click here” carry no topic signal.Internal links serve crawling and relevance at the same time. They create the paths Googlebot follows, and their anchor text and context signal topical relationships. A page can be indexed with weak internal links, but it usually performs better with them.A common issue is adding new pages to the sitemap without linking to them from anywhere. The sitemap helps discovery, but internal links tell Google the page matters.Step 7: Test Mobile Usability and JavaScript RenderingTo check whether Google can render your JavaScript content, run a live test in Search Console’s URL Inspection tool, open “View tested page,” and compare the rendered HTML and screenshot with what visitors see. Content missing from the rendered HTML may not be indexed.Confirm mobile parity. Google predominantly uses the mobile version of a page for indexing. seoTitle: How to Do a Technical SEO Audit (Free Checklist) - FrameCipher
content:
You published the pages, tuned the keywords, and still nothing shows up in search. Often the problem isn’t the content. Google may be unable to crawl a page, may choose not to index it, or may see something different from what visitors see.

Learning how to do a technical SEO audit gives you a repeatable way to find those problems using free tools and a fixed order of checks. This guide covers ten steps, each with a pass criterion, a severity level, and the tool that checks it. The quick answer comes first.

How to Do a Technical SEO Audit: Quick Answer

To do a technical SEO audit, crawl your site, check which pages Google has indexed, review robots.txt and sitemaps, fix status codes and redirects, resolve canonical conflicts, review internal links, test mobile rendering, measure Core Web Vitals, check HTTPS, and validate structured data, in that order.

Definition: Technical SEO audit
 A technical SEO audit is a systematic review of a website’s crawlability, indexability, rendering, structure, security, and performance, designed to find the issues that stop search engines from discovering, understanding, and ranking its pages.

The ten steps in order:

  1. Crawl your website to build a URL inventory.

  2. Check which pages Google has indexed in Search Console.

  3. Audit robots.txt and XML sitemaps for access and discovery problems.

  4. Fix status codes, redirects, and broken links.

  5. Resolve canonical and duplicate URL issues.

  6. Review site structure, internal links, and orphan pages.

  7. Test mobile usability and JavaScript rendering.

  8. Measure Core Web Vitals and page speed.

  9. Check HTTPS and website security.

  10. Validate structured data.

The order follows how Google processes a site: it crawls a URL, indexes it, renders it, and then ranks it. A page that cannot be crawled cannot be indexed, and a page that cannot be indexed gains nothing from speed or schema fixes. That is why indexing checks come before performance checks.

What You Need Before You Start: Free Audit Tools

A free technical SEO audit needs Google Search Console, PageSpeed Insights, Lighthouse, Chrome DevTools, a free crawler such as the free version of Screaming Frog SEO Spider, and optionally Ahrefs Webmaster Tools. Together they cover indexing, site-wide status data, rendering, and performance.

Tool

What it checks

Free limits

Google Search Console

Indexing status, robots.txt report, sitemaps, Core Web Vitals field data, security issues

Free; requires verifying site ownership

PageSpeed Insights

Core Web Vitals field data (when available) and lab diagnostics

Free; one URL at a time

Lighthouse

Lab data for performance, accessibility, and SEO basics

Free; built into Chrome DevTools

Chrome DevTools

Rendered HTML, network requests, mobile emulation

Free; built into Chrome

Screaming Frog SEO Spider

Status codes, canonicals, titles, headings, crawl depth, broken links

Free version crawls up to 500 URLs, per the vendor’s documentation

Ahrefs Webmaster Tools

Site audit and backlink data for sites you own

Free for verified sites

Google Analytics 4

Landing pages that receive traffic

Free

When choosing tools, ask two questions. Does the tool use Google’s own data? Does it show page-level detail you can act on?

A crawler shows what could be wrong, while Search Console shows what Google actually sees. One mistake people often make is trusting a crawler report alone. The audit needs both, because a crawler cannot tell you which URLs Google has chosen to index.

Before starting, verify your site in Search Console and confirm GA4 is collecting data. Without verification, the indexing and Core Web Vitals checks later in the audit are not available.

Step 1: Crawl Your Website

A site crawl is an automated scan that follows links from your homepage and records each URL’s status code, title, canonical, indexability, and depth. In an audit, the crawl produces the URL inventory that every later step checks against.

  1. Open your crawler and enter your homepage URL, using the full https:// version.

  2. Add your sitemap if the tool allows it, so pages with no internal links are included.

  3. Run the crawl and wait for it to finish. On large sites, a free crawler may stop at its URL cap.

  4. Export the key columns: URL, status code, indexability, canonical, title, and crawl depth.

  5. Save the export as your baseline. You will re-crawl later to confirm fixes worked.

On a large site, sample by page template instead of by URL count. Check one page each from the homepage, category, blog post, and product templates. One broken template can affect thousands of pages, so a single fix at the template level often resolves them all.

A common mistake is crawling only the homepage and a few links, then treating the result as the whole site. If the crawl hits a limit, note which templates it did not reach.

Step 2: Check Which Pages Google Has Indexed

To check whether pages are indexed, open the Page indexing report in Google Search Console, review the indexed and not-indexed totals, and then run URL Inspection on individual pages. Compare Google’s indexed list against the indexable URLs from your crawl to find gaps.

Status

What it means

Next action

Crawled – currently not indexed

Google fetched the page but chose not to index it

Review content quality and uniqueness; check for duplicates

Discovered – currently not indexed

Google knows the URL but has not crawled it yet

Add internal links; confirm it is in the sitemap

Excluded by ‘noindex’ tag

The page tells Google not to index it

Remove the tag if the page should rank

Blocked by robots.txt

Google is not allowed to crawl the URL

Edit robots.txt if the page should be crawled

Duplicate, Google chose a different canonical

Google picked another URL as the main version

Align canonicals, redirects, and internal links

Page with redirect

The URL redirects elsewhere

Usually fine; make sure internal links point to the final URL

The most damaging edge case is a noindex tag left on after launch. A staging setting carries into production, and important pages quietly drop out of search while the team keeps publishing.

“Crawled – currently not indexed” is often a content-quality signal rather than a technical bug. Google may judge the page thin, repetitive, or too similar to another page. Fixing it usually means improving the page, not editing code.

To compare lists, export your crawl’s indexable URLs and the indexed URLs from Search Console. Pages in the first list but missing from the second are your investigation queue.

Step 3: Audit Robots.txt and XML Sitemaps

Check that robots.txt does not block important pages or CSS and JavaScript files, and that your XML sitemap lists only canonical, indexable URLs that return a 200 status. Robots.txt controls crawl access, while the sitemap helps search engines discover pages.

Robots.txt

  • Look for accidental disallows. A Disallow: / copied from a staging site blocks the entire site.

  • Check for blocked resources. Blocking CSS or JavaScript files can stop Google from rendering pages correctly.

  • Use the robots.txt report in Search Console to confirm Google can fetch and parse the file.

  • Keep the file small. According to Google’s documentation, Google processes only the first 500 KiB of a robots.txt file.

XML sitemaps

  • List only indexable URLs. Remove redirected, noindexed, canonicalized, and error URLs.

  • Respect the limits. Per Google Search Central documentation, one sitemap file can hold up to 50,000 URLs or 50 MB uncompressed. Larger sites use a sitemap index.

  • Submit the sitemap in Search Console and check for errors.

  • Keep lastmod honest. Update it only when page content changes.

A noindex tag and a robots.txt block conflict with each other. Google cannot see a noindex tag on a page it is not allowed to crawl, so the URL may stay in the index. To remove a page from search, allow crawling and use noindex.

Step 4: Fix Status Codes, Redirects, and Broken Links

The HTTP status codes that matter most in a technical SEO audit are 200 (OK), 301 (permanent redirect), 302 (temporary redirect), 404 (not found), 410 (gone), and 5xx (server errors). Each tells search engines how to treat a URL, and 5xx errors are the most urgent.

Code

Meaning

Action

200

Page loads normally

No action; confirm it is the intended URL

301

Permanent redirect

Fine when pointing to the correct final URL

302

Temporary redirect

Change to 301 if the move is permanent

404

Page not found

Fix only if the page has links, traffic, or a replacement

410

Permanently removed

Use for pages you deliberately deleted

5xx

Server error

Fix immediately; check hosting and server logs

Redirect chains happen when one URL redirects to another that redirects again. Loops send crawlers in circles. Per Google’s documentation, Googlebot follows up to 10 redirect hops, but shorter chains are faster and safer. Aim for one hop from the old URL to the final one.

A soft 404 is a page that shows “not found” content but returns a 200 status. Search Console reports these, and the fix is to return a real 404 or restore the content.

Update internal links to point to the final URL instead of relying on redirects. Redirects are a safety net, not a substitute for correct links.

Not every 404 needs fixing. According to Google’s guidance, 404 errors on URLs that never existed or have no value do not harm the rest of your site. Prioritize broken URLs that have backlinks, internal links, or traffic.

Step 5: Resolve Canonical and Duplicate URL Issues

A canonical tag is an HTML element that tells search engines which URL is the preferred version when the same or very similar content exists at several addresses. It consolidates ranking signals onto one URL and reduces duplicate indexing.

Common causes of duplicate URLs:

  • www vs non-www: www.example.com and example.com both load.

  • HTTP vs HTTPS: both versions return a page.

  • Trailing slashes: /shoes and /shoes/ serve the same content.

  • URL parameters: filters, sorting, and tracking codes create new URLs.

A mini example: if example.com/shoes?color=red shows a filtered view of the main shoes page, its canonical tag should point to example.com/shoes. The main page should carry a self-referencing canonical that points to itself.

Google treats canonicals as a hint, not a command. When signals conflict, such as a canonical pointing one way, a redirect another, and the sitemap listing a third URL, Google may choose a different URL than you intended. Search Console reports this as “Duplicate, Google chose different canonical than user.”

Teams often run into this after a migration, when old canonicals are copied across. The fix is consistency: the canonical, internal links, redirects, and sitemap should all name the same URL.

Step 6: Review Site Structure, Internal Links, and Orphan Pages

An orphan page is a page with no internal links pointing to it, which makes it hard for search engines to discover and weakens its authority. To find one, compare the URLs in your sitemap and GA4 landing pages against the URLs your crawler reached through links.

  1. Check crawl depth. Pages many clicks from the homepage are typically discovered and revisited less reliably. Google publishes no fixed depth limit, so use depth as a relative signal and look for important pages buried deeper than they should be.

  2. Find orphan pages. Pages in the sitemap or in GA4 landing page reports that your crawl did not reach through links are orphan candidates.

  3. Check hub and cluster links. Each main topic page should link to its supporting articles, and those articles should link back.

  4. Review anchor text. Descriptive anchors tell search engines what the target page is about. Anchors like “click here” carry no topic signal.

Internal links serve crawling and relevance at the same time. They create the paths Googlebot follows, and their anchor text and context signal topical relationships. A page can be indexed with weak internal links, but it usually performs better with them.

A common issue is adding new pages to the sitemap without linking to them from anywhere. The sitemap helps discovery, but internal links tell Google the page matters.

Step 7: Test Mobile Usability and JavaScript Rendering

To check whether Google can render your JavaScript content, run a live test in Search Console’s URL Inspection tool, open “View tested page,” and compare the rendered HTML and screenshot with what visitors see. Content missing from the rendered HTML may not be indexed.

  1. Confirm mobile parity. Google predominantly uses the mobile version of a page for indexing. Text, links, structured data, and images present on desktop should also appear on mobile.

  2. Compare raw and rendered HTML. In Chrome, view the page source (raw HTML), then inspect the page in DevTools (rendered HTML). Important text and links should appear in the rendered version.

  3. Run the URL Inspection live test. Open “View tested page” to see the rendered HTML and a screenshot of what Googlebot received.

  4. Check blocked resources. If the screenshot looks broken, a blocked script or stylesheet may be the cause.

  5. Test with JavaScript disabled in DevTools to learn how much content depends on it.

Raw source can look nearly empty while the rendered page is fine, and the reverse is also possible. Content that appears only after a user clicks, scrolls, or logs in may never be seen by Googlebot.

Google has retired its standalone Mobile-Friendly Test and the Mobile Usability report. Use Lighthouse, DevTools device emulation, and URL Inspection instead.

Step 8: Measure Core Web Vitals and Page Speed

Good Core Web Vitals scores, per Google’s web.dev documentation, are a Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) of 2.5 seconds or less, an Interaction to Next Paint (INP) of 200 milliseconds or less, and a Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) of 0.1 or less, each measured at the 75th percentile of page loads.

Metric

“Good” threshold

Common causes of poor scores

Typical fix

LCP (loading)

≤ 2.5 seconds

Slow server response, oversized hero images, render-blocking scripts

Compress images, use caching or a CDN, defer non-critical scripts

INP (responsiveness)

≤ 200 ms

Heavy JavaScript, long tasks blocking the main thread

Reduce and split scripts, remove unused plugins

CLS (visual stability)

≤ 0.1

Images without dimensions, late-loading ads, font swaps

Set width and height on media, reserve space for embeds

Field data and lab data measure different things. Field data comes from real users and appears in the Search Console Core Web Vitals report and at the top of PageSpeed Insights. Lab data comes from a simulated test, such as Lighthouse. The two can disagree, and low-traffic sites may have no field data at all. In that case, use lab data to find fixes and re-check field data later.

Audiences in markets like Bangladesh often browse mainly on mobile devices and slower connections, so speed problems that look minor on a fast office network can matter more. For international audiences, hosting location and a CDN can also affect server response and LCP.

One mistake people often make is chasing a perfect 100 Lighthouse score. The goal is passing the three thresholds for real users, not maximizing a lab number.

Step 9: Check HTTPS and Website Security

HTTPS issues that affect SEO include an expired or invalid SSL certificate, HTTP pages that do not redirect to HTTPS, mixed content (insecure resources on secure pages), and security warnings reported in Search Console. Each can trigger browser warnings or split ranking signals between URL versions.

  • Certificate validity: the certificate is current and covers the exact domain, including www if used. Pass: the browser shows no warning.

  • Redirects: every HTTP URL redirects with a 301 to its HTTPS equivalent. Pass: no HTTP page returns a 200.

  • Mixed content: images, scripts, or stylesheets load over http:// on an HTTPS page. Pass: the DevTools console shows no mixed-content warnings.

  • Search Console security issues: check for hacked content or malware flags. Pass: no issues listed.

Certificate renewals that lapse silently are a common cause of sudden traffic drops. Browsers show a full-page warning, and most visitors leave. Set a calendar reminder or enable auto-renewal, and confirm it actually works.

Step 10: Validate Structured Data

To check structured data for errors, paste the URL into Google’s Rich Results Test to see which rich result types are eligible, then use the Schema Markup Validator to check general Schema.org syntax. Fix errors first and review warnings by importance.

  • Test key templates: one article, one product, and the homepage are usually enough to catch template-wide problems.

  • Match visible content. Markup should describe what users can actually see on the page. Google’s structured data guidelines warn against marking up content that isn’t visible.

  • Choose types that fit. Article, Organization, BreadcrumbList, Product, and LocalBusiness are the most commonly useful.

  • Check Search Console enhancement reports for errors across the whole site.

Valid markup does not guarantee rich results. Google decides whether to show them based on eligibility, quality, and the query. Treat schema as a way to clarify meaning, not a switch that forces a result.

How to Prioritize Technical SEO Issues

Fix issues in this order: first those that block indexing, then those that waste crawling or split ranking signals, then those that affect page experience, and last cosmetic warnings. Impact on whether pages can appear in search should decide the order, not the number of warnings.

Severity

Examples

When to fix

Critical

Noindex on important pages, robots.txt blocks, 5xx errors, expired certificate

Immediately

High

Redirect chains and loops, canonical conflicts, orphan pages with value

Within the current work cycle

Medium

Core Web Vitals failures, mixed content, missing structured data

Planned and scheduled

Low

Only when convenient

For a quick impact-versus-effort check, sort fixes into four groups: high impact and low effort (do first, such as removing an accidental noindex), high impact and high effort (plan, such as a speed overhaul), low impact and low effort (batch later), and low impact and high effort (usually skip).

Beginners can follow the severity order and stop there. Advanced teams can also weight by traffic and revenue, fixing template-level issues on pages that already earn impressions.

Not everything needs fixing. A handful of old 404s with no links or traffic can be left alone, and chasing every crawler warning is a common way to burn time without improving visibility.

Free Technical SEO Audit Checklist

A technical SEO audit checklist covers crawl access, indexing, status codes, canonicals, internal links, rendering, Core Web Vitals, HTTPS, and structured data. Each check needs a tool, a pass criterion, and a severity level so you know when it is complete and how urgent a failure is.

Keep a simple findings log with five columns: URL, issue, severity, owner, and status. It turns the audit from a one-time report into a work list you can track and re-check.

Common Technical SEO Audit Mistakes

The most common technical SEO audit mistakes are checking page speed before indexing, treating every crawler warning as an error, ignoring Search Console data, blocking resources in robots.txt, auditing only the homepage, and never re-crawling after fixes. Most of them come from skipping the order of dependencies.

Mistake

Why it hurts

Fix

Auditing speed before indexing

Fast pages that aren’t indexed still get no traffic

Confirm indexing first

Treating every crawler warning as an error

Wastes time on low-impact items

Score each finding by severity

Crawlers can’t show what Google chose to index

The scenario to watch for is polishing pages Google cannot see. A team rewrites titles and content on pages that are noindexed, blocked, or not indexed, and nothing improves. Re-crawling after each batch of fixes confirms the change worked and caught nothing new.

When to Do It Yourself and When to Get Help

A free audit is usually enough for small sites with no indexing errors. Hire a professional for technical SEO when pages stay unindexed after basic fixes, when a migration or redesign is planned, or when speed and rendering problems trace back to code, hosting, or a JavaScript framework you cannot change yourself.

Do it yourself when:

  • The site is small, and Search Console shows no major indexing errors.

  • Problems are limited to titles, links, sitemaps, and settings you can edit in your CMS.

  • You can re-run the checklist after each change.

Bring in a specialist when:

  • The site is large, uses a JavaScript framework, or relies on custom code.

  • Traffic dropped after a migration, redesign, or platform change.

  • Indexing or Core Web Vitals problems persist after the basic fixes.

Framecipher offers technical SEO services for teams that want a developer-level review and implementation. Sites targeting the US, UK, Canada, and Australia together may also need hreflang and regional setup reviewed, which is easy to get wrong without experience.

Conclusion

A technical SEO audit works best as an ordered process rather than a long list of checks. Start with what Google can crawl and index, move to rendering and speed, and score each finding by how much it affects visibility.

Three practical takeaways:

  1. Audit in dependency order: indexing first, then rendering, then speed and structured data.

  2. Score every finding by severity so you fix the few issues that matter and skip the noise.

  3. Re-crawl and re-check Search Console after fixes to confirm they worked.

Your next step: run the free checklist on your ten most important pages and log each finding by severity. If critical issues remain after the basic fixes, a professional audit from Framecipher can help you find the cause and plan the repair.

title: Local SEO for Small Businesses: A Beginner's Guide
metaDescription: Learn local SEO step by step: set up your Google Business Profile, fix NAP, earn reviews, and rank in Google Maps. Free checklist for small business owners.
content:
Local SEO for small businesses is the work of making a business appear when nearby customers search on Google Search and Google Maps. It starts with a verified Google Business Profile, accurate business details, local keywords, and genuine reviews, then adds measurement so you can see which actions produce calls and visits.

Picture someone searching 'plumber near me' with a burst pipe at 7 a.m. They often choose from the first few businesses on the map. A business missing from that list never gets the chance to compete.

This guide walks through five steps, written for owners in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, and Bangladesh. It follows Google's own Business Profile and Search Central documentation, and it ends with a 30-day checklist.

What Is Local SEO and How Does It Work?

Definition: Local SEO. Local SEO is the practice of optimizing a business's online presence so it appears in location-based searches on Google Search and Google Maps. It combines a verified Google Business Profile, consistent business details, local keywords, reviews, and local links to attract customers searching for nearby products or services.

When a search carries local intent, such as 'dentist near me' or 'bakery in Dhaka', Google often shows a map with a short list of businesses, usually called the Local Pack, alongside standard web results. The searcher taps a listing, which opens the business in Google Maps, and then calls, requests directions, or visits the website. Each step depends on the one before it: local search intent triggers the Local Pack, the Local Pack draws on Business Profiles, and the profile determines what the customer can do next.

Proximity matters because Google compares where the searcher is, or the location named in the query, with where each business is. Two equally strong businesses will usually rank differently for people standing on opposite sides of a city.

Aspect

Local SEO

Traditional SEO

Main goal

Appear in the Local Pack, Maps, and local organic results

Rank web pages for topics regardless of location

Key asset

Google Business Profile plus website

Website pages

Role of location

Searcher location and business proximity affect results

Location usually matters less

Typical success metric

Calls, direction requests, visits

Organic sessions, rankings

Main trust signals

Reviews, NAP consistency, citations

Backlinks, content depth

One mistake people often make is treating local SEO as a website-only project. A well-built site with no verified Business Profile typically misses the Local Pack, because the pack lists profiles, not web pages.

How Google Ranks Local Businesses

Quick answer: Google ranks local businesses using three factors: relevance, distance, and prominence. Relevance measures how well a profile matches the search, distance measures how far the business is from the searcher or the location named in the query, and prominence reflects how well known the business is across the web.

According to Google's Business Profile Help documentation, these three factors are combined to produce local results, and standard SEO best practices also apply to local ranking. The practical value is knowing which factor you can influence.

Factor

What Google looks at

Your control

Action

Relevance

How well the profile and website match the search

High

Choose accurate categories, list services, write a clear description, align website content

Distance

Searcher location compared with the business location

Low

Keep the address accurate and service areas honest

Prominence

Information from across the web, including reviews, links, articles, and directories

Medium

Earn reviews, fix citations, build local links

A common issue is trying to change distance, for example by moving the map pin or listing a fake address. This violates Google's guidelines and risks suspension. A better way to think about it is that in dense areas a nearby competitor may win on distance alone, so the realistic response is to compete on relevance and prominence, and to target more specific queries where fewer businesses are competing.

Step 1: Claim and Optimize Your Google Business Profile

Quick answer: To rank higher on Google Maps, claim and verify a Google Business Profile, choose the most accurate primary category, complete every field, keep name, address, and phone details consistent across the web, and earn genuine customer reviews. Relevance, distance, and prominence determine position, so the first three actions are within a beginner's control.

Work through the profile in this order:

  1. Search before creating. Look up your business name in Google Maps. If a profile already exists, claim it instead of creating a second one, since duplicates split reviews and signals.

  2. Verify. Google offers several verification methods, and which ones appear depends on the business type and location. An unverified profile typically cannot manage reviews or appear reliably in local results.

  3. Choose the primary category. Search your main service, open the top-ranked profiles, and note the primary category each uses. Pick the one that matches your main revenue service most specifically. Google allows additional categories, up to nine, but adding broad ones dilutes relevance.

  4. Use the real business name. Google's guidelines require the name to match how the business appears in the real world. Adding keywords such as a city or service to the name can lead to suspension.

  5. Write the description. Google allows up to 750 characters. Describe what you do, who you serve, and where, in plain language, without links or keyword lists.

  6. Add services, hours, photos, and attributes. Include holiday hours, list each service, and upload real photos of the premises, team, and work.

  7. Use posts and Q&A. Posts and questions help customers, though they usually matter less than the fields above.

Google does not publish how much weight each field carries, so the table below reflects typical impact, not official weighting.

Priority

Field

Why it matters

High

Primary category

Sets relevance for the searches you can appear in

High

Name, address, phone, website

Defines the business and must match the website

High

Hours and services

Prevents wasted visits and supports relevance

Medium

Description, photos, attributes

Helps customers choose and adds context

Lower

Posts and Q&A

Useful for engagement, less likely to change rankings

Local note: Address formats differ by country. US addresses end with a city, state, and ZIP code. UK addresses use a postcode, Canadian addresses use a letter-number postal code, and Australian addresses use a state and four-digit postcode. In Bangladesh, addresses often rely on house, road, block, and area names, sometimes with a landmark. Whatever the format, copy it exactly as it appears on the website and every other listing. Verification options also vary by country, so confirm what Google offers for your location.

Step 2: Do Local Keyword Research and Build Location-Aware Pages

Quick answer: Local keyword research means combining a service, a location, and an intent modifier, such as 'emergency plumber Leeds' or 'graphic designer Dhaka', then validating demand with Google Keyword Planner, Google Trends, and Search Console. The best targets match what customers actually type, not how the business describes itself.

Follow this process:

  1. List services and areas. Write every service you sell and every town, neighborhood, or region you serve.

  2. Combine them into patterns. The common patterns are service plus city, service plus neighborhood, and specialty plus city.

  3. Treat 'near me' differently. Google decides 'near me' results mainly from the searcher's location, so repeating the phrase on a page rarely helps. Clear address details and defined service areas do more.

  4. Validate demand. Google Keyword Planner shows search volume ranges and requires a Google Ads account. Google Trends compares interest across regions and over time. Search Console shows queries your site already receives.

  5. Map each keyword to one page. The home page, a service page, or an area page should each own a distinct set of terms.

  6. Apply the terms on the page. Use them in the title tag, H1, opening paragraph, image alt text, and a short section about the area served. Put the full name, address, and phone number in the footer or a contact block.

Business type

Pattern

Example

Best page

Storefront café

Service plus neighborhood

specialty coffee Fitzroy

Home or location page

Service-area plumber

Service plus city

emergency plumber Leeds

Service page

Clinic

Specialty plus city

pediatric dentist Calgary

Service page

Home-based freelancer

Service plus region

graphic designer Dhaka

Home or services page

The practical difference between a useful location page and a thin one is whether it would still read the same after the city name is swapped. Google's spam policies treat pages created mainly to capture similar searches as doorway pages. For a single-location business, one 'areas we serve' section plus one page per main service is typically enough. Create a separate area page only when it holds distinct content, such as local examples, a team that works there, or details that differ from other areas.

Step 3: Fix Your NAP and Build Local Citations

Quick answer: NAP consistency means a business's name, address, and phone number appear identically on its website, Google Business Profile, and every directory listing. Consistent details help search engines match listings to one business and reduce the risk of duplicate listings splitting reviews and ranking signals across several profiles.

A local citation is any online mention of a business's name, address, and phone number, usually in a directory or platform. The chain works like this: consistent NAP makes citations trustworthy, trustworthy citations feed prominence, and prominence supports Maps rankings.

  1. Write the canonical NAP. Record the exact name, address format, primary phone number with country code, and website URL in one document.

  2. Audit. Search for your business name, old addresses, and old phone numbers. A tool such as BrightLocal can speed this up, and manual searching works too. In most cases, a wrong phone number or an old address causes more trouble than a minor abbreviation such as 'St.' versus 'Street'.

  3. Fix core platforms first. Start with Google Business Profile, Bing Places, Apple Business Connect, and your Facebook page.

  4. Add relevant directories. Choose national directories and industry-specific ones that match your category.

  5. Resolve duplicates. Google's Business Profile Help describes how to report duplicate or incorrect listings.

Country

Examples to check first

Note

United States

Bing Places, Apple Business Connect, Yelp, Facebook

Directory strength varies by industry

United Kingdom

Bing Places, Apple Business Connect, Yell, trade-specific directories

Trade and professional bodies often matter more than general directories

Canada

Bing Places, Apple Business Connect, Yellow Pages Canada, Facebook

Keep the business name in one consistent language form

Australia

Bing Places, Apple Business Connect, Yellow Pages Australia, True Local, Hotfrog

Use state and postcode consistently

Bangladesh

Google Maps listing, Facebook business page, local directories that already rank for your category

Keep the address style identical everywhere

Directory popularity changes, so confirm a directory is still active before submitting.

A citation priority approach avoids wasted effort: core platforms first, niche directories second, and low-quality directories skipped. Paid packages that push your details to hundreds of unknown sites rarely justify the cost, and they can create inconsistent listings that are hard to clean up later.

Step 4: Earn and Manage Customer Reviews

Quick answer: To get more Google reviews, ask satisfied customers shortly after a positive experience, give them a direct link or QR code to the review form, and respond to every review. Google's policies prohibit offering incentives for reviews and selectively requesting reviews only from happy customers, so requests should go to all customers.

Google states that review count and score factor into local ranking, so reviews connect directly to prominence, and prominence connects to Maps position and click-through.

Ask-timing framework. Ask at the moment the customer can see the value delivered: after a repair is completed and checked, after a haircut when the customer says thanks, or after a project handover. This typically produces better responses than a request weeks later. Use the channel customers already use with you, such as SMS, WhatsApp, email, or a QR code on a receipt or counter card. The direct review link is available from your Business Profile's share options.

Response templates

Positive review: Thank you, [Name]. We're glad the [specific service] went well. We look forward to seeing you again.

Negative review: Thank you for telling us, [Name]. We're sorry the [specific issue] fell short. Please contact us at [phone or email] so we can look into it and put it right.

Keep replies short, specific, and free of personal details. Avoid arguing in public, since the reply is read by future customers as much as by the reviewer.

A common issue is review gating, which means sending happy customers to Google and unhappy ones to a private form. Google's policies prohibit it. Fake reviews, paid reviews, and reviews from staff or family also violate policy and can lead to removal or suspension. Ask everyone, accept the mix, and respond to all of it.

Step 5: Build Local Authority with Links and Mentions

Quick answer: Small businesses build local links by earning mentions from organizations that already know them: chambers of commerce, sponsored teams or events, supplier and partner sites, local news, and community blogs. A handful of relevant local links typically outweighs dozens of unrelated directory or paid links.

Local links lead to authority, and authority supports prominence. Five low-cost ways to earn them:

  • Join a local business association or chamber of commerce and make sure the member listing links to your site.

  • Sponsor a local team, event, or charity that publishes sponsors on its own website.

  • Ask suppliers and partners to list you on their 'where to buy' or 'approved installers' pages.

  • Share genuinely newsworthy updates with local news outlets, such as an opening, a community project, or a useful local finding.

  • Publish something locally useful, such as a seasonal checklist for homeowners in your area, that schools, councils, or community groups may reference.

What to avoid: paid link packages, large-scale link exchanges, and offers of 'hundreds of local backlinks'. Google's spam policies cover link schemes, and low-quality links add risk without adding trust. The tradeoff is time. Local links accumulate slowly, so they work best as a steady monthly habit.

Storefront vs Service-Area Business: What Changes?

Quick answer: Service-area businesses serve customers at the customer's location rather than at a public premises, so they typically hide their street address on Google Business Profile and define service areas instead. Storefront businesses display their address because customers visit in person during staffed business hours.

The decision comes down to three questions:

  1. Do customers visit your address during stated hours? If yes, you are a storefront and the address is shown.

  2. Do you travel to customers and receive no visitors? If yes, you are a service-area business and the address is hidden.

  3. Do both happen? Then you are a hybrid, which shows the address and also lists service areas.

In practice, a café is a storefront. A plumber is a service-area business. A home-based freelancer who works online or at client sites is also typically a service-area business, with the home address kept private. A clinic that sees patients on site is a storefront, and becomes a hybrid if it also makes home visits.

Setup item

Storefront

Service-area business

Address on profile

Shown

Hidden when no customers visit

Service areas

Optional

Required, and Google limits how many can be listed

Website pages

Location page plus service pages

Service pages, with area pages only where content is distinct

Distance in rankings

Based on the visible address

In most cases still based on the verified location, even though it is hidden

Verification

At the premises

At the business address, which can be harder for home-based businesses

A common mistake is listing a PO box or virtual office as a storefront. Google's guidelines do not allow it. The tradeoff for service-area businesses is reach: ranking far from the base location is difficult, so a realistic service area works better than a very large one.

Mobile Experience and Local Schema Markup

Quick answer: LocalBusiness schema is structured data from the Schema.org vocabulary that describes a business's name, address, phone number, hours, and location in a format search engines can read. Google's documentation treats it as markup that can help Google understand business details on a page.

Most local searches happen on phones, and Google uses the mobile version of a site for indexing. Mobile problems usually cost leads before rankings, so check these points:

  • Tappable phone number. Use a tel: link, not plain text or an image.

  • Text, not images. Keep address, hours, and prices as text.

  • Fast loading. Google's Core Web Vitals guidance treats a Largest Contentful Paint of 2.5 seconds or less as good.

  • No blocking popups. This usually breaks when a banner covers the call button.

Minimal schema checklist (no code needed at this stage):

  • Use the most specific type available, such as Dentist or Plumber, instead of the generic LocalBusiness.

  • Include name, address, telephone, URL, opening hours, and geographic coordinates.

  • Add the logo or an image, and sameAs links to your Business Profile and social profiles.

  • Add areaServed if you are a service-area business.

  • Match every detail to what is visible on the page and what appears on Google Business Profile.

Validate with Google's Rich Results Test or the Schema Markup Validator. One mistake people often make is marking up reviews the business wrote about itself. Google's guidelines do not allow self-serving reviews in LocalBusiness markup.

How to Measure Local SEO Results

Quick answer: Local SEO success is measured with calls, direction requests, website clicks, Google Business Profile views, review count and rating, local keyword rankings, and leads or sales from the website. Business Profile Performance, Search Console, and Google Analytics 4 report most of these at no cost, and rank-tracking tools cover local positions.

Measurement works only if the baseline is recorded before changes begin. Note this month's calls, direction requests, website clicks, review count, and Search Console impressions before touching the profile.

The connection runs from Search Console impressions to GA4 key events to revenue. Each metric below maps to one business outcome.

Metric

Where to find it

What it tells you

Business Profile Performance, plus a tracking number if used

Whether the profile produces phone leads

Business Profile Performance

Intent to visit, most relevant for storefronts

How much profile traffic reaches the site

Organic visibility for local terms

GA4

Form submissions and phone-link clicks that count as leads

Business Profile

Position by location, usually a paid feature

Two practical details help. First, add UTM parameters to the website link on your profile so GA4 can separate profile visits from other traffic. Second, if you use call tracking, add the tracking number as an additional phone number and keep the main number as primary, so the NAP stays consistent.

A common issue is tracking rankings alone. Rankings vary by the searcher's location, and a position on its own does not show whether anyone called. Set a monthly routine: record the metrics, compare with the previous month and the same month last year to account for seasonality, and log what you changed.

Common Local SEO Mistakes (and How to Fix Them)

Quick answer: The most common local SEO mistakes are adding keywords to the business name, choosing inaccurate categories, leaving duplicate listings, buying or gating reviews, using one thin page for every city, and ignoring reviews. Each one weakens relevance or prominence, and most can be fixed without paid tools.

Mistake

Why it hurts

Fix

Your 30-Day Local SEO Checklist

Quick answer: Beginners should start local SEO by claiming and verifying the Google Business Profile, then correcting name, address, and phone details, adding the right categories, and requesting reviews. These tasks cost nothing, apply to every business type, and form the base that website work, citations, and links build on.

Is local SEO free? Local SEO is free to start: claiming a Google Business Profile, completing it, requesting reviews, and using Search Console and Google Analytics 4 cost nothing. Paid costs typically come from rank-tracking tools, citation services, advertising, or hiring an agency, and none are required for the core setup.

Google publishes no official timeline for ranking changes. Profile edits can appear within days, but movement against established competitors typically takes weeks to months, and results vary by competition, category, and location. Nobody can promise a specific position.

A note on what to skip: paid directory blasts, daily posting for its own sake, and chasing rankings for areas outside your real service area.

Conclusion

Local SEO for small businesses comes down to a short list of steady habits, done in the right order. Three takeaways matter most:

  1. Start with a verified, fully completed Google Business Profile. Every other step builds on it.

  2. Keep business details consistent and earn reviews steadily. Consistent NAP and genuine reviews support prominence over time.

  3. Measure calls and direction requests, not just rankings. Visibility only matters when it produces customers.

faqs.question: How long does local SEO take to work?
faqs.answer: Local SEO typically takes several weeks to a few months to show clear movement, though Google publishes no official timeline. Profile changes can appear within days, while ranking gains depend on competition, category, location, review volume, and how complete the existing profile is. Treat any guaranteed position as a warning sign.

faqs.question: Do I need a website for local SEO?
faqs.answer: A website is not strictly required because a verified Google Business Profile can appear in Maps and Local Pack results on its own. A website still strengthens relevance, supports conversion tracking, and gives local keywords, service pages, and schema a place to live, so most businesses benefit from having one.

faqs.question: How much does local SEO cost?
faqs.answer: The core steps cost nothing: Google Business Profile, Search Console, and Google Analytics 4 are free. Costs typically come from optional tools, paid directory packages, website changes, or hiring an agency, and they vary widely by market and scope. A small business can usually complete the foundation with time alone.

faqs.question: Can I do local SEO myself?
faqs.answer: Yes, most beginners can complete the foundation themselves: profile setup, NAP cleanup, review requests, and basic on-page changes. Professional help becomes worth considering when competition is intense, a profile is suspended or duplicated, several locations are involved, or time is a constraint.

faqs.question: Why am I not showing in Google Maps?
faqs.answer: Common causes are an unverified or suspended profile, an inaccurate or overly broad primary category, a missing or inconsistent address, a searcher located far from the business, and stronger competitor prominence. Check verification status first, then categories, then whether the address and service areas meet Business Profile guidelines.

faqs.question: Do reviews really affect local rankings?
faqs.answer: Yes. Google states that review count and score factor into local ranking as part of prominence, and that positive, high-quality reviews can improve a business's visibility. Reviews also influence whether people click, call, or visit, so their value extends beyond ranking itself.
